name: Food Allergies
overview: A food allergy happens when the immune system mistakes a harmless food — like peanuts, milk, eggs, or shellfish — for a threat and overreacts. Reactions range from an itchy mouth or hives to a severe, life-threatening reaction called anaphylaxis. There's no cure yet, so the main strategy is avoiding the trigger food and carrying epinephrine if your doctor recommends it. Most people manage food allergies well with a clear plan, careful label-reading, and the right medicines on hand.
symptoms: Tingling or itching in the mouth
Swelling of the lips, face, or throat

drugs.name: Cetirizine (Zyrtec) / Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
drugs.note: Calms mild reactions like itching and hives.

drugs.name: Epinephrine (EpiPen)
drugs.note: Lifesaving shot for severe reactions — use it and call 911.

drugs.name: Omalizumab (Xolair)
drugs.note: A shot that can soften reactions to accidental exposures.

drugs.name: Peanut oral immunotherapy (Palforzia)
drugs.note: Builds tolerance to peanut in tiny daily steps under a doctor's care.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, throat tightness, or widespread hives after eating means use epinephrine right away and call 911 — don't wait to see if it passes.

name: Anaphylaxis
overview: Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction that comes on fast — usually within minutes of exposure to a trigger like certain foods, insect stings, medicines, or latex. It can cause trouble breathing, a sudden drop in blood pressure, and fainting, so it is always a medical emergency. The good news: epinephrine works quickly when given right away, and most people recover fully. Anyone at risk should carry two epinephrine auto-injectors and know how to use them.
symptoms: Throat tightness or a hoarse voice
Dizziness or fainting from a drop in blood pressure
A sudden sense that something is very wrong

drugs.name: Epinephrine (EpiPen)
drugs.note: The first and most important treatment — use it immediately.

drugs.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
drugs.note: Helps with hives and itching after epinephrine is given.

drugs.name: Albuterol
drugs.note: Eases wheezing once epinephrine is on board.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: Sometimes given afterward to calm lingering inflammation.

redFlags: Anaphylaxis is always an emergency — use epinephrine immediately and call 911, even if symptoms seem to improve.

resources.label: Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America

name: Drug Allergies
prevalence: ~1 in 10 Americans report a drug allergy
overview: A drug allergy is when the immune system reacts to a medicine as if it were harmful, causing hives, itching, swelling, or — rarely — a severe reaction called anaphylaxis. Antibiotics like penicillin are the most common culprits. The key is knowing which medicine caused the reaction and telling every doctor and pharmacist about it. Interestingly, many people who think they're allergic to penicillin actually aren't, so allergy testing can sometimes safely open up more treatment options.
symptoms: Swelling of the face or throat

drugs.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
drugs.note: Relieves hives and itching from mild reactions.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone cream
drugs.note: Soothes itchy skin rashes.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: For stronger or more widespread reactions.

drugs.name: Epinephrine (EpiPen)
drugs.note: For severe whole-body reactions — use it and call 911.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a blistering, peeling rash after taking a medicine means use epinephrine if you have it and call 911 or get to the ER now.

resources.label: American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology

name: Insect Sting Allergy
overview: Most insect stings cause only temporary pain, redness, and swelling. But in people with an insect sting allergy, the immune system overreacts to venom from bees, wasps, hornets, yellow jackets, or fire ants — sometimes causing a dangerous whole-body reaction. Anyone who has had a serious reaction should carry epinephrine and see an allergist. Venom immunotherapy (allergy shots) can greatly lower the risk of future severe reactions, making time outdoors feel a lot safer.
symptoms: Large swelling that spreads beyond the sting site
Hives or itching far from the sting
Swelling of the face, lips, or throat

drugs.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
drugs.note: Eases itching and swelling from most stings.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone cream
drugs.note: Calms redness and itching at the sting site.

drugs.name: Epinephrine (EpiPen)
drugs.note: Lifesaving treatment for a severe allergic reaction.

drugs.name: Venom immunotherapy
drugs.note: Gradually retrains the immune system to tolerate insect venom.

redFlags: Hives all over, trouble breathing, throat swelling, or dizziness after a sting means use epinephrine if you have it and call 911.

resources.label: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology

name: Peripheral Artery Disease
aka: PAD, poor circulation in the legs
prevalence: ~6.5 million U.S. adults age 40 and older
overview: Peripheral artery disease happens when fatty plaque narrows the arteries that carry blood to your legs. The classic sign is cramping or aching in the calves when you walk that eases with rest. It matters because the same plaque buildup often affects the heart and brain, raising the risk of heart attack and stroke. The encouraging news: walking programs, quitting smoking, and common medicines can ease symptoms and protect your arteries.
symptoms: Leg cramping or aching when walking that eases with rest
Numbness or weakness in the leg
A foot or lower leg that feels cold
Sores on the toes or feet that heal slowly
Shiny skin or hair loss on the lower legs

drugs.name: Atorvastatin (Lipitor)
drugs.note: Lowers cholesterol and slows plaque buildup.

drugs.name: Aspirin (low-dose)
drugs.note: Helps keep clots from forming in narrowed arteries.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel (Plavix)
drugs.note: An alternative or addition to aspirin.

drugs.name: Cilostazol
drugs.note: Can help you walk farther without pain.

drugs.name: Supervised walking program
drugs.note: A proven first-line treatment that builds pain-free walking distance.

redFlags: A leg or foot that suddenly turns cold, pale, numb, or intensely painful may mean an artery is completely blocked — call 911 or get to the ER right away.

name: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
aka: Blood clot in a deep vein
prevalence: Up to ~900,000 Americans affected each year (DVT and pulmonary embolism combined)
overview: Deep vein thrombosis is a blood clot that forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg, causing swelling and pain. It matters because a piece of the clot can break loose and travel to the lungs — a pulmonary embolism, which can be life-threatening. Surgery, long trips, pregnancy, and long stretches of sitting raise the risk. Blood thinners treat most clots, and most people recover fully.
symptoms: Leg pain or cramping, often starting in the calf
Skin that feels warm over the sore area
Red or discolored skin on the leg
A vein that feels hard or tender to the touch

drugs.name: Apixaban (Eliquis)
drugs.note: A common blood-thinning pill for treating clots.

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto)
drugs.note: Another widely used pill-based blood thinner.

drugs.name: Warfarin (Coumadin)
drugs.note: An older blood thinner that needs regular blood tests.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin (Lovenox)
drugs.note: An injectable thinner often used when treatment starts.

drugs.name: Compression stockings
drugs.note: Can ease leg swelling while you recover.

redFlags: Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood can mean the clot has traveled to the lungs — call 911 immediately.

name: Heart Palpitations & Arrhythmias
prevalence: About 1 in 20 U.S. adults has some type of arrhythmia
overview: Heart palpitations are the feeling that your heart is racing, fluttering, or skipping beats. Most of the time they're harmless and triggered by stress, caffeine, or lack of sleep. Sometimes, though, they signal an arrhythmia — a glitch in the heart's electrical rhythm — that deserves a checkup. Doctors can usually pinpoint the cause with a simple heart-rhythm recording, and most rhythm problems today are very treatable.
symptoms: A fluttering, pounding, or racing feeling in the chest
A flip-flop sensation in the chest or neck
Episodes triggered by stress, caffeine, or poor sleep

drugs.name: Metoprolol (Lopressor)
drugs.note: Slows the heart and calms racing rhythms.

drugs.name: Diltiazem (Cardizem)
drugs.note: Another common option to control heart rate.

drugs.name: Flecainide
drugs.note: Helps keep certain abnormal rhythms in check.

drugs.name: Catheter ablation
drugs.note: A procedure that can correct many arrhythmias at their source, often permanently.

redFlags: Palpitations that come with chest pain, fainting, or severe shortness of breath need emergency care — call 911.

name: Heart Valve Disease
overview: Your heart has four valves that keep blood flowing in the right direction. Heart valve disease means one of them has become stiff (stenosis) or leaky (regurgitation), forcing the heart to work harder. It often develops slowly with age, so many people don't notice it at first — a doctor may hear a murmur before any symptoms appear. Mild cases just need monitoring, and advanced ones can be fixed with valve repair or replacement.
symptoms: Shortness of breath with activity or when lying down
Feeling tired or worn out more easily
A heart murmur heard by a doctor

drugs.name: Furosemide (Lasix)
drugs.note: Eases fluid buildup and shortness of breath.

drugs.name: Metoprolol (Lopressor)
drugs.note: Lightens the heart's workload.

drugs.name: Warfarin (Coumadin)
drugs.note: Prevents clots, especially with mechanical valves.

drugs.name: Valve repair or replacement
drugs.note: The definitive fix for advanced valve disease, often done through a small catheter.

redFlags: Sudden severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or fainting needs emergency care — call 911.

name: Aortic Aneurysm
prevalence: About 200,000 new U.S. diagnoses each year
overview: An aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the wall of the aorta, the body's largest artery, which runs from the heart through the chest and belly. Most aneurysms grow slowly and cause no symptoms, so they're often found during scans done for other reasons. Small ones are simply watched with regular imaging, and larger ones can be repaired before they become dangerous. Controlling blood pressure and not smoking help keep them from growing.
symptoms: Often no symptoms at all — found on a scan
A deep, steady ache in the belly or back
A pulsing feeling near the belly button (abdominal type)
Chest or upper back pain (chest type)
Hoarseness or trouble swallowing with large chest aneurysms

drugs.name: Metoprolol (Lopressor)
drugs.note: Lowers blood pressure to ease stress on the aorta.

drugs.name: Losartan (Cozaar)
drugs.note: Another option for keeping pressure off the aortic wall.

drugs.name: Atorvastatin (Lipitor)
drugs.note: Helps slow artery disease throughout the body.

drugs.name: Endovascular or open surgical repair
drugs.note: Repairs larger aneurysms before they can rupture.

redFlags: Sudden, severe, tearing pain in the chest, back, or belly — especially with lightheadedness or fainting — may mean a rupture; call 911 immediately.

name: Acne
overview: Acne happens when oil and dead skin cells clog pores, letting bacteria grow and cause pimples, blackheads, and sometimes deeper painful bumps. It's the most common skin condition in the United States and is especially common during the teen years, though plenty of adults get it too. Acne isn't caused by poor hygiene, and it's very treatable — most people see real improvement with over-the-counter products or prescription medicines, which also helps prevent scarring.
symptoms: Dark spots or scars after breakouts heal

drugs.name: Benzoyl peroxide
drugs.note: Kills acne bacteria and unclogs pores.

drugs.name: Adapalene (Differin)
drugs.note: Once prescription-only, now available over the counter.

drugs.name: Salicylic acid
drugs.note: Found in washes and spot treatments to clear pores.

drugs.name: Clindamycin (topical)
drugs.note: Prescription gel often paired with benzoyl peroxide.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.note: Short-term pill for moderate, inflamed acne.

redFlags: Severe acne that appears suddenly along with fever and joint pain is rare but serious — seek same-day medical care.

name: Rosacea
overview: Rosacea is a long-term skin condition that causes flushing, redness, and small bumps, usually across the cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead. It's most common in adults over 30 with fair skin, and flares can be triggered by sun, heat, spicy food, alcohol, or stress. There's no cure, but creams, pills, and simple trigger-avoidance keep it well controlled for most people — and it isn't contagious or caused by anything you did wrong.
symptoms: Lasting redness across the cheeks and nose
Small red bumps that can look like acne

drugs.name: Metronidazole (MetroGel)
drugs.note: The most common first cream for bumps and redness.

drugs.name: Azelaic acid (Finacea)
drugs.note: Calms bumps and evens out skin tone.

drugs.name: Ivermectin (Soolantra)
drugs.note: Targets the skin mites that can worsen rosacea.

drugs.name: Doxycycline (Oracea)
drugs.note: A pill option for flares that creams alone can't control.

redFlags: If your eyes become painful, very red, or your vision blurs, see a doctor promptly — untreated eye rosacea can damage sight.

name: Shingles
overview: Shingles is a painful, blistering rash caused by the chickenpox virus waking up after lying quiet in your nerves for years. It usually shows up as a stripe of blisters on one side of the body. Anyone who has had chickenpox can get shingles, and the risk rises after age 50. Starting antiviral pills within 72 hours speeds healing and lowers the chance of lasting nerve pain — and a vaccine prevents most cases.
symptoms: Burning, tingling, or stabbing pain on one side of the body
A stripe of fluid-filled blisters appearing a few days later
Itching and skin so sensitive that clothing hurts

drugs.name: Valacyclovir (Valtrex)
drugs.note: Speeds healing when started within 72 hours of the rash.

drugs.name: Acyclovir
drugs.note: An older, lower-cost antiviral option.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen / Ibuprofen
drugs.note: Eases rash pain while it heals.

drugs.name: Gabapentin
drugs.note: Helps if nerve pain lingers after the rash clears.

drugs.name: Shingrix
drugs.note: Prevents most cases in adults 50 and older.

redFlags: A shingles rash on your face or near an eye — or any rash with confusion or severe headache — needs emergency care to protect your vision and brain, so go to the ER.

name: Hives (Urticaria)
prevalence: about 1 in 5 people at some point in life
overview: Hives are raised, itchy welts that appear suddenly on the skin and often move around or change shape within hours. They're usually a reaction to something — a food, a medicine, an infection, or even heat or stress — though often no cause is ever found. Most cases clear on their own within a day or two, and antihistamines calm the itch. Hives that keep returning for more than six weeks are called chronic hives.
symptoms: Raised, itchy welts that can be red or skin-colored
Welts that change shape, move around, or fade within hours
Swelling of the lips or eyelids (angioedema)
Flares triggered by heat, stress, or pressure on the skin

drugs.name: Cetirizine (Zyrtec)
drugs.note: A non-drowsy first choice for calming the itch.

drugs.name: Loratadine (Claritin)
drugs.note: Another non-drowsy daily option.

drugs.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
drugs.note: Works quickly but causes drowsiness.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: A short course for severe outbreaks.

redFlags: Hives with swelling of the tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or dizziness can be anaphylaxis — use epinephrine if you have it and call 911.

resources.label: Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America

name: Fungal Skin Infections (Ringworm & Athlete's Foot)
prevalence: about 1 in 4 people get athlete's foot at some point
overview: Fungal skin infections like ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by tiny fungi that thrive on skin, especially in warm, damp spots like the feet, groin, and skin folds. Despite the name, no worm is involved — ringworm simply describes the ring-shaped rash it leaves. These infections are very common, mildly contagious, and usually easy to clear with over-the-counter antifungal creams. Keeping skin clean and dry goes a long way toward preventing them from coming back.
symptoms: A ring-shaped, scaly rash with a clearer center (ringworm)
Itchy, peeling skin between the toes (athlete's foot)
Redness and cracking in the groin or skin folds
Thick, discolored nails when nails are involved

drugs.name: Terbinafine (Lamisil) cream
drugs.note: A go-to over-the-counter cream for athlete's foot and ringworm.

drugs.name: Clotrimazole (Lotrimin)
drugs.note: A widely used cream for most fungal rashes.

drugs.name: Miconazole
drugs.note: Common in powders and sprays that help keep damp areas dry.

drugs.name: Terbinafine (oral)
drugs.note: A prescription pill for stubborn nail or scalp infections.

redFlags: Spreading redness, warmth, pus, fever, or red streaks can mean a bacterial infection has set in on top of the fungus — seek same-day care.

resources.label: MedlinePlus — Fungal Skin Infections (Ringworm & Athlete's Foot)

name: Hair Loss
overview: Hair loss is extremely common and has many causes — heredity is the biggest one, but stress, illness, thyroid problems, low iron, and certain medicines can also trigger shedding. Hereditary hair loss (male- or female-pattern) develops gradually and affects roughly 80 million Americans. While that kind doesn't reverse on its own, medicines can slow it down and regrow some hair, and shedding from stress or illness usually grows back once the trigger passes.
symptoms: Gradual thinning on top of the head
More hair than usual on your pillow, brush, or shower drain

drugs.name: Minoxidil (Rogaine)
drugs.note: Over-the-counter foam or liquid used by men and women.

drugs.name: Finasteride (Propecia)
drugs.note: A prescription pill for male-pattern hair loss.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.note: Often prescribed for female-pattern hair loss.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injections
drugs.note: Used for patchy hair loss from alopecia areata.

redFlags: Sudden hair loss in clumps along with rash, scalp pain, fever, or feeling ill can signal an underlying illness — seek same-day care.

name: Type 1 Diabetes
overview: Type 1 diabetes happens when the immune system mistakenly destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin — the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into the body's cells. Without insulin, blood sugar climbs to dangerous levels, so people with type 1 take insulin every day for life. It often starts in childhood but can appear at any age. With modern insulins, pumps, and glucose monitors, people with type 1 live full, active lives.

drugs.name: Rapid-acting insulin (Humalog, NovoLog)
drugs.note: Taken with meals to handle blood-sugar rises from food.

drugs.name: Long-acting insulin (Lantus, Tresiba)
drugs.note: Provides a steady background level of insulin all day.

drugs.name: Insulin pump with glucose monitor
drugs.note: Many people use these instead of multiple daily shots.

drugs.name: Glucagon (Baqsimi, Gvoke)
drugs.note: Raises blood sugar fast during a severe low.

redFlags: Vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity-smelling breath, or confusion can signal diabetic ketoacidosis — call 911 or go to the ER.

name: Prediabetes
overview: Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet high enough to count as type 2 diabetes. It's remarkably common — more than 1 in 3 American adults have it, and most don't know. The encouraging news: prediabetes is often reversible. Losing a modest amount of weight, moving more, and eating better can bring blood sugar back to normal and cut your risk of developing diabetes roughly in half.
symptoms: Usually no symptoms — most people don't know they have it
Darkened, velvety skin patches on the neck or armpits
Often found only through a routine blood test

drugs.name: Lifestyle changes
drugs.note: Losing 5-7% of body weight and walking regularly can cut diabetes risk about in half.

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.note: Sometimes prescribed when lifestyle changes alone aren't enough.

drugs.name: Diabetes Prevention Program
drugs.note: A CDC-backed group program proven to lower the risk of type 2 diabetes.

redFlags: Extreme thirst, constant urination, blurry vision, or unplanned weight loss can mean diabetes has developed — seek same-day care.

name: Hyperthyroidism (Overactive Thyroid)
aka: Overactive thyroid, Graves' disease (most common cause)
overview: Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid gland in your neck makes too much thyroid hormone, putting your whole body into overdrive — heart racing, weight dropping, hands shaky, mind anxious. The most common cause is Graves' disease, where the immune system overstimulates the thyroid. It's very treatable: medicines can slow hormone production, and radioactive iodine or surgery offer lasting fixes. Most people feel like themselves again once hormone levels are back to normal.
symptoms: Weight loss despite a good appetite
Sweating more and feeling too warm
Bulging or irritated eyes (with Graves' disease)

drugs.name: Methimazole (Tapazole)
drugs.note: First-choice pill that slows the thyroid's hormone production.

drugs.name: Propranolol / Atenolol
drugs.note: Calms a racing heart and tremors while other treatment takes effect.

drugs.name: Radioactive iodine
drugs.note: A one-time capsule that shrinks overactive thyroid tissue.

drugs.name: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
drugs.note: An alternative used in early pregnancy or when methimazole isn't tolerated.

redFlags: Fever, a very fast heartbeat, and confusion or agitation can signal thyroid storm, a rare emergency — call 911 or go to the ER.

name: Low Testosterone
prevalence: About 2 in 100 men (more common with age)
overview: Testosterone naturally declines as men get older, but when levels drop well below normal, it can sap energy, mood, sex drive, and muscle strength. A simple morning blood test confirms the diagnosis — symptoms alone aren't enough, since fatigue and low libido have many causes, including poor sleep, stress, and depression. When true low T is found, testosterone replacement can help many men feel better, though it requires ongoing monitoring by a doctor.
symptoms: Loss of muscle and increased body fat

drugs.name: Testosterone gel (AndroGel)
drugs.note: A daily gel rubbed into the skin — one of the most common forms.

drugs.name: Testosterone injection (Depo-Testosterone)
drugs.note: A shot given every one to two weeks.

drugs.name: Testosterone patch (Androderm)
drugs.note: Worn on the skin and changed daily.

drugs.name: Lifestyle changes
drugs.note: Weight loss, exercise, and better sleep can raise levels naturally.

redFlags: If you're on testosterone therapy and develop chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, or a swollen painful leg, call 911 — these can signal a blood clot.

name: Metabolic Syndrome
overview: Metabolic syndrome isn't one disease — it's a cluster of risk factors that tend to show up together: a large waistline, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, high triglycerides, and low "good" cholesterol. Having three or more raises your risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes. About 1 in 3 American adults has it. The hopeful part: the same lifestyle changes — losing weight, exercising, eating better — improve all five at once.
symptoms: Usually no obvious symptoms day to day
High blood sugar on lab tests
High triglycerides or low "good" HDL cholesterol

drugs.name: Lifestyle changes
drugs.note: Weight loss, exercise, and healthier eating improve every part of the syndrome.

drugs.name: Atorvastatin (Lipitor)
drugs.note: Lowers cholesterol to protect the heart.

drugs.name: Lisinopril
drugs.note: A common choice for bringing blood pressure down.

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.note: Helps control blood sugar when it starts creeping up.

redFlags: Chest pain, sudden weakness on one side, face drooping, or trouble speaking can signal a heart attack or stroke — call 911 right away.

name: Sinus Infection (Sinusitis)
prevalence: About 29 million U.S. adults each year
overview: A sinus infection happens when the moist air spaces behind your cheeks, nose, and forehead get inflamed and filled with mucus, usually after a cold. That causes facial pressure, stuffiness, and thick drainage. Most cases are caused by viruses and clear up on their own within a week or two — antibiotics only help when bacteria are to blame. Rest, fluids, saline rinses, and time are often the best medicine.
symptoms: Pressure or pain around the cheeks, eyes, or forehead

drugs.name: Saline nasal rinse
drugs.note: Flushes out mucus and soothes irritated sinuses.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) / Ibuprofen (Advil)
drugs.note: Eases facial pain, pressure, and fever.

drugs.name: Fluticasone (Flonase)
drugs.note: Calms swelling inside the nose.

drugs.name: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed)
drugs.note: Short-term relief for a stuffed-up nose.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin)
drugs.note: For bacterial infections that aren't improving on their own.

redFlags: Swelling or redness around an eye, vision changes, severe headache with a stiff neck, or confusion can mean the infection is spreading — go to the ER.

name: Ear Infections
prevalence: About 5 out of 6 children have one by age 3
overview: Ear infections happen when fluid builds up behind the eardrum and gets infected, usually during or after a cold. They're one of the most common reasons young children see a doctor, though adults get them too. The classic signs are ear pain, fussiness, and trouble hearing. Many mild cases clear up on their own within a few days; antibiotics help when symptoms are severe or don't improve.
symptoms: Ear pain, or tugging at the ear in young kids

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: First step for easing ear pain and fever.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another good option for pain and fever.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.note: The usual first choice when an antibiotic is needed.

drugs.name: Ear tubes (tympanostomy)
drugs.note: A minor surgery for kids who get infection after infection.

redFlags: A high fever with a stiff neck, swelling or redness behind the ear, or a child who is unusually drowsy or hard to wake needs emergency care.

name: Tinnitus (Ringing in the Ears)
overview: Tinnitus is hearing a sound — ringing, buzzing, or hissing — that isn't coming from the outside world. It's usually linked to age-related hearing loss, loud-noise exposure, or even earwax buildup, and it's rarely a sign of something dangerous. There's no single cure, but many people find real relief with hearing aids, sound machines, and counseling approaches that teach the brain to tune the noise out.
symptoms: Ringing, buzzing, hissing, or humming in the ears
Sound seems louder in quiet places, especially at night
Often comes along with some hearing loss
May be constant or come and go

drugs.name: Hearing aids
drugs.note: Boosting outside sound often makes the ringing fade into the background.

drugs.name: Sound therapy (white-noise machines)
drugs.note: Masks the ringing, especially at bedtime.

drugs.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
drugs.note: Teaches the brain to react less to the sound.

drugs.name: Earwax removal
drugs.note: A quick fix when built-up wax is the cause.

redFlags: Tinnitus in only one ear, tinnitus that pulses with your heartbeat, or ringing with sudden hearing loss needs prompt evaluation — sudden hearing loss is a same-day emergency.

name: Hearing Loss
prevalence: About 1 in 8 Americans age 12 and older
overview: Hearing loss usually creeps in slowly, most often from aging, years of loud noise, or both. You might find yourself asking people to repeat things or turning the TV up. It matters because untreated hearing loss can lead to isolation and strain relationships, but today's options — including hearing aids sold over the counter — are better and easier to get than ever. A simple hearing test is the place to start.
symptoms: Trouble following conversations in noisy places
Turning the TV or phone volume way up

drugs.name: Hearing aids
drugs.note: The main treatment — now sold over the counter for mild-to-moderate loss.

drugs.name: Earwax removal
drugs.note: A quick fix when wax buildup is the culprit.

drugs.name: Assistive listening devices
drugs.note: Phone captions and TV streamers fill in the gaps.

drugs.name: Cochlear implant
drugs.note: For severe loss when hearing aids aren't enough.

redFlags: Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears is a medical emergency — seek care the same day, because quick treatment can sometimes save your hearing.

name: Vertigo (BPPV)
prevalence: About 2 in 100 adults at some point
overview: BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo — that sudden spinning feeling. It happens when tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear drift out of place, confusing your balance sensors whenever you roll over in bed or tilt your head. The spells are brief but can be intense. The good news: a simple series of head movements called the Epley maneuver fixes most cases, often in a single office visit.
symptoms: Brief spinning sensation triggered by head movements
Worse when rolling over in bed or looking up
Episodes usually last less than a minute

drugs.name: Epley maneuver
drugs.note: Guided head movements that put the loose crystals back in place — the main treatment.

drugs.name: Meclizine (Antivert)
drugs.note: Short-term help for the dizzy, queasy feeling.

drugs.name: Vestibular rehab exercises
drugs.note: Retrains your balance system if symptoms linger.

drugs.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
drugs.note: For severe nausea during bad spells.

redFlags: Vertigo with double vision, slurred speech, weakness, numbness, or a sudden severe headache could be a stroke — call 911.

name: Tonsillitis
prevalence: Millions of U.S. cases a year, mostly kids ages 5–15
overview: Tonsillitis means the tonsils — the two soft pads at the back of the throat — are inflamed, usually from a virus and sometimes from strep bacteria. It brings a sore throat, trouble swallowing, fever, and swollen glands. Viral cases get better with rest and fluids; strep needs antibiotics. Tonsil-removal surgery is reserved these days for kids and adults who get infections again and again.
symptoms: Sore throat and pain when swallowing
Red, swollen tonsils, sometimes with white patches
Swollen, tender glands in the neck

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases throat pain and fever.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another solid choice for pain and fever.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin / Penicillin
drugs.note: First choice when a strep test comes back positive.

drugs.name: Tonsillectomy
drugs.note: Surgery to remove the tonsils after frequent repeat infections.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, drooling, inability to swallow, a muffled voice, or severe one-sided throat swelling can signal a serious abscess — go to the ER.

name: Laryngitis
prevalence: Very common — about 1 in 3 people have a voice problem at some point
overview: Laryngitis is irritation of the voice box (larynx) that leaves you hoarse, raspy, or barely able to speak above a whisper. Most cases come from a cold virus or from overusing your voice — think cheering at a game — and they heal on their own within a week or two. Resting your voice and drinking plenty of fluids speeds things along; antibiotics almost never help. Hoarseness that drags on for weeks deserves a checkup.
symptoms: Tickling or raw feeling in the throat

drugs.name: Voice rest and fluids
drugs.note: The main treatment — give the vocal cords time to heal.

drugs.name: Humidifier or steam
drugs.note: Moist air soothes an irritated voice box.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) / Ibuprofen (Advil)
drugs.note: Eases throat soreness.

drugs.name: Omeprazole (Prilosec)
drugs.note: Helps when stomach acid reflux is behind chronic hoarseness.

redFlags: Hoarseness with trouble breathing, noisy breathing, or trouble swallowing needs ER care right away; hoarseness lasting more than three weeks needs a doctor's look.

name: Crohn's Disease
overview: Crohn's disease is a long-term condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks the digestive tract, causing inflammation anywhere from mouth to anus — most often the end of the small intestine. It tends to flare up and then quiet down. There's no cure yet, but modern medicines can calm the inflammation, ease symptoms like pain and diarrhea, and help many people stay in remission for years.
symptoms: Belly pain and cramping (often lower right)
Mouth sores or sores near the anus

drugs.name: Prednisone / Budesonide
drugs.note: Calms flares quickly; not meant for long-term use.

drugs.name: Azathioprine (Imuran)
drugs.note: Quiets the immune system to help keep remission going.

drugs.name: Adalimumab (Humira)
drugs.note: Blocks a key inflammation signal; given as a shot.

drugs.name: Infliximab (Remicade)
drugs.note: IV medicine for moderate-to-severe disease.

redFlags: Severe belly pain with fever, repeated vomiting, or a swollen, rigid abdomen could mean a blockage or tear — go to the ER.

name: Ulcerative Colitis
overview: Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease that affects only the colon (large intestine), where the immune system causes sores and inflammation in the inner lining. Symptoms come in flares — bloody diarrhea, cramping, urgency — followed by calm stretches. It often starts in young adulthood. While there's no cure short of surgery, today's medicines keep many people symptom-free for long periods.
symptoms: Diarrhea, often with blood or pus

drugs.name: Mesalamine (Lialda)
drugs.note: The usual first medicine for mild-to-moderate UC.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: Short courses bring flares under control.

drugs.name: Azathioprine (Imuran)
drugs.note: Helps maintain remission between flares.

drugs.name: Infliximab (Remicade)
drugs.note: For moderate-to-severe UC that other medicines don't control.

redFlags: Heavy rectal bleeding, high fever, or severe pain with a swollen belly can signal a dangerous complication — go to the ER.

name: Celiac Disease
overview: Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten — a protein in wheat, barley, and rye. When someone with celiac eats gluten, their immune system damages the lining of the small intestine, blocking the absorption of nutrients. It can cause digestive trouble, fatigue, anemia, and more. The good news: a strict gluten-free diet lets the intestine heal, and most people feel dramatically better within weeks to months.

drugs.name: Strict gluten-free diet
drugs.note: The only proven treatment — it lets the intestine heal.

drugs.name: Vitamin & mineral supplements
drugs.note: Replace iron, vitamin D, and other nutrients while the gut recovers.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: Rarely needed, for celiac that doesn't respond to the diet.

redFlags: Relentless diarrhea or vomiting with dizziness, confusion, or other signs of severe dehydration needs same-day medical care.

name: Gallstones
overview: Gallstones are hardened lumps of digestive fluid — usually cholesterol — that form in the gallbladder, a small pouch under the liver. Many people have them and never know it. Trouble starts when a stone blocks a duct, causing sudden pain in the upper right belly, often after a fatty meal. If stones keep causing attacks, removing the gallbladder is a safe, common surgery, and most people live normally without it.
symptoms: Sudden pain in the upper right belly
Pain spreading to the right shoulder or back

drugs.name: Gallbladder removal (cholecystectomy)
drugs.note: The standard fix for stones that cause attacks, usually done with small incisions.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain during a gallstone attack.

drugs.name: Ursodiol (Actigall)
drugs.note: Can slowly dissolve some cholesterol stones when surgery isn't an option.

redFlags: Belly pain lasting more than a few hours with fever, chills, or yellowing skin or eyes means go to the ER.

name: Peptic Ulcer
prevalence: About 1 in 10 Americans during their lifetime
overview: A peptic ulcer is an open sore in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine. Most are caused by a common bacterium called H. pylori or by regular use of pain relievers like ibuprofen — not by stress or spicy food, as once believed. The burning belly pain can be miserable, but most ulcers heal completely with a few weeks of medicine.

drugs.name: Omeprazole (Prilosec)
drugs.note: Cuts stomach acid so the ulcer can heal.

drugs.name: Antibiotic combo (amoxicillin + clarithromycin)
drugs.note: Clears H. pylori, the bacteria behind most ulcers.

drugs.name: Famotidine (Pepcid)
drugs.note: A gentler acid reducer, used when medicines like omeprazole aren't a fit.

drugs.name: Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol)
drugs.note: Coats the ulcer and helps fight H. pylori.

redFlags: Vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, or sudden severe belly pain are emergencies — call 911 or get to the ER.

name: Fatty Liver Disease
overview: Fatty liver disease means extra fat has built up in the liver, usually linked to weight, diabetes, or high cholesterol rather than alcohol. Most people have no symptoms and find out through routine blood work. Caught early, it's very treatable — losing even 5 to 10 percent of body weight can clear much of the fat. Left alone, it can slowly progress to inflammation and scarring in some people.
symptoms: Dull ache in the upper right belly
Abnormal liver tests on routine blood work

drugs.name: Weight loss & exercise
drugs.note: The most effective treatment — even modest weight loss helps the liver.

drugs.name: Vitamin E
drugs.note: Sometimes used for liver inflammation, under a doctor's guidance.

drugs.name: Pioglitazone (Actos)
drugs.note: An option for some people with diabetes and liver inflammation.

drugs.name: Resmetirom (Rezdiffra)
drugs.note: A newer prescription for moderate-to-advanced liver scarring.

redFlags: Yellowing skin or eyes, a swollen belly, or new confusion can signal serious liver trouble — seek emergency care.

name: Diverticulitis
overview: Diverticulitis happens when small pouches that form in the colon wall (called diverticula) become inflamed or infected, causing pain — usually in the lower left belly — plus fever or nausea. The pouches themselves are very common with age and usually harmless. Most flares are mild and clear up with rest, a temporary liquid diet, and sometimes antibiotics, though severe or repeated attacks occasionally need surgery.
symptoms: Steady pain, usually in the lower left belly
Tenderness when the belly is pressed

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin)
drugs.note: A common choice when antibiotics are needed for a flare.

drugs.name: Metronidazole (Flagyl) + ciprofloxacin
drugs.note: A frequently used pair for people who can't take penicillin.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Preferred over NSAIDs, which can irritate the colon.

drugs.name: Clear-liquid diet
drugs.note: Rests the colon for a few days during a mild flare.

redFlags: Worsening pain, high fever, or vomiting that keeps you from holding down fluids needs emergency care — go to the ER.

name: Lactose Intolerance
overview: Lactose intolerance means the body doesn't make enough lactase, the enzyme that digests the natural sugar in milk. After dairy, the undigested lactose ferments in the gut, causing gas, bloating, cramps, and diarrhea. It's extremely common — and it's not dangerous, and not the same as a milk allergy. Most people manage it easily by adjusting how much dairy they eat, choosing lactose-free products, or taking lactase tablets before meals.

drugs.name: Lactase tablets (Lactaid)
drugs.note: Taken with dairy to help digest the lactose.

drugs.name: Lactose-free dairy products
drugs.note: Same nutrition as regular dairy, minus the lactose.

drugs.name: Calcium & vitamin D supplements
drugs.note: Fill the nutritional gap if you cut back on dairy.

redFlags: Blood in the stool, unintended weight loss, or symptoms that continue even off dairy aren't from lactose intolerance — seek same-day care.

name: HIV
overview: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system, the body's defense against infection. It spreads through certain body fluids, most often during sex or by sharing needles. Without treatment it can lead to AIDS, but today daily medicine can keep the virus so low it's undetectable — letting people live long, healthy lives and avoid passing it to others. There is no cure yet, but treatment works.

drugs.name: Bictegravir combo (Biktarvy)
drugs.note: A common single-pill daily treatment.

drugs.name: Dolutegravir (Tivicay)
drugs.note: Blocks the virus from copying itself.

drugs.name: Emtricitabine/tenofovir (Truvada)
drugs.note: Also used as PrEP to prevent infection.

drugs.name: Cabotegravir (Apretude)
drugs.note: A shot option given every two months.

redFlags: High fever, trouble breathing, confusion, or a severe new infection can signal a dangerous complication — seek same-day care or go to the ER.

name: Hepatitis B
overview: Hepatitis B is a viral infection that inflames the liver. It spreads through blood and body fluids, including during birth, sex, or sharing needles. Many adults clear it on their own, but some develop a long-term (chronic) infection that can quietly damage the liver over years. A safe vaccine prevents it, and when long-term treatment is needed, medicines can control the virus and protect the liver.
symptoms: Belly pain on the upper right side

drugs.name: Tenofovir (Viread)
drugs.note: A common daily pill for chronic infection.

drugs.name: Entecavir (Baraclude)
drugs.note: Lowers the virus and protects the liver.

drugs.name: Hepatitis B vaccine
drugs.note: Safely prevents infection before exposure.

drugs.name: Peginterferon
drugs.note: An injectable option for some patients.

redFlags: Severe belly pain, vomiting blood, deep yellowing of the skin, or confusion can mean serious liver trouble — go to the ER.

name: Hepatitis C
overview: Hepatitis C is a viral infection of the liver that spreads mainly through blood, often from sharing needles. It usually causes no symptoms for years, so many people don't know they have it until a routine blood test finds it. Left untreated it can scar the liver over time. The good news: newer pills now cure most people in just 8 to 12 weeks, which is why testing matters.
symptoms: Belly pain on the upper right side

drugs.name: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (Epclusa)
drugs.note: A common pill that cures most people.

drugs.name: Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Mavyret)
drugs.note: A short 8-week cure for many.

drugs.name: Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni)
drugs.note: Another effective curative regimen.

redFlags: Vomiting blood, severe belly pain, deep jaundice, or confusion can signal advanced liver damage — go to the ER.

name: Lyme Disease
overview: Lyme disease is a bacterial infection spread by the bite of an infected blacklegged (deer) tick. An early sign is often a spreading, sometimes bullseye-shaped rash, along with flu-like aches. Caught early, it's usually cured with a short course of antibiotics. If untreated, it can spread to the joints, heart, or nervous system, so prompt treatment after a known tick bite or rash matters.
symptoms: Spreading rash, sometimes shaped like a bullseye

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.note: First-choice treatment for most adults.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.note: Often used for kids or in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Cefuroxime (Ceftin)
drugs.note: An alternative for some patients.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.note: For more serious nervous-system or heart cases.

redFlags: Fainting, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, severe headache with a stiff neck, or facial drooping need urgent care — go to the ER.

name: Tuberculosis
overview: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that usually attacks the lungs. It spreads through the air when someone with active TB coughs or sneezes. Many people carry it in a sleeping (latent) form with no symptoms and can't spread it, but it can wake up later. Active TB causes a lasting cough and other symptoms. It's curable, but treatment takes several months of antibiotics taken exactly as directed.
symptoms: A cough lasting three weeks or more

drugs.name: Isoniazid
drugs.note: A core TB drug, often part of combos.

drugs.name: Rifampin
drugs.note: Used with other drugs to kill the bacteria.

drugs.name: Pyrazinamide
drugs.note: Part of the standard early treatment phase.

drugs.name: Ethambutol
drugs.note: Added to prevent drug resistance.

redFlags: Coughing up large amounts of blood, severe trouble breathing, or chest pain with high fever needs emergency care — call 911 or go to the ER.

name: STIs (Chlamydia, Gonorrhea & Syphilis)
prevalence: ~2.4 million U.S. cases reported per year
overview: Chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis are common infections passed through sex. Many people have no symptoms, which is why they spread easily and why regular testing matters. When symptoms do appear, they may include discharge, burning, or sores. Left untreated they can cause lasting harm, including infertility, but all three are curable with antibiotics. Treating partners and getting retested helps stop reinfection.
symptoms: Unusual discharge from the penis or vagina
Sores, bumps, or a rash in the genital area

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.note: First-choice shot for gonorrhea.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.note: Standard treatment for chlamydia.

drugs.name: Penicillin G (Bicillin)
drugs.note: The main treatment for syphilis.

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.note: An alternative for some infections.

redFlags: Severe pelvic pain with fever, testicle pain and swelling, or symptoms during pregnancy need same-day care — call your doctor or go to the ER.

name: Genital Herpes
overview: Genital herpes is a very common infection caused by the herpes simplex virus and spread through skin-to-skin contact during sex. It can cause outbreaks of painful blisters or sores, though many people have mild symptoms or none at all. There's no cure, but the virus stays manageable: daily or as-needed medicine eases outbreaks, shortens them, and lowers the chance of passing it to a partner.
symptoms: Painful blisters or sores in the genital area
Itching or tingling before an outbreak
Flu-like aches during the first outbreak

drugs.name: Valacyclovir (Valtrex)
drugs.note: A convenient once- or twice-daily option.

drugs.name: Acyclovir (Zovirax)
drugs.note: Treats outbreaks and can be taken daily.

drugs.name: Famciclovir (Famvir)
drugs.note: Another antiviral for outbreaks.

redFlags: A severe first outbreak with trouble peeing, a stiff neck with bad headache, or sores during late pregnancy need prompt care — call your doctor or go to the ER.

name: Kidney Stones
prevalence: About 1 in 10 Americans over a lifetime
overview: Kidney stones are hard, pebble-like pieces of mineral that form inside the kidneys, usually when urine becomes too concentrated. Small stones often pass on their own, though the trip can be very painful. Larger ones sometimes need a procedure to break them up or remove them. The good news: most stones cause no lasting damage, and drinking plenty of water is the single best way to prevent new ones.
symptoms: Sharp pain in the side or back that comes in waves
Pain spreading to the lower belly or groin

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil) / Naproxen (Aleve)
drugs.note: Eases the pain while a stone passes.

drugs.name: Tamsulosin (Flomax)
drugs.note: Relaxes the urinary tract so the stone passes more easily.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: A gentler option when NSAIDs aren't a good fit.

drugs.name: Potassium citrate
drugs.note: Makes urine less likely to form certain types of stones.

drugs.name: Shock wave lithotripsy
drugs.note: Breaks larger stones into pieces small enough to pass.

redFlags: Stone pain with fever and chills, or being unable to urinate at all, can mean a dangerous blocked or infected kidney — go to the ER.

name: Polycystic Kidney Disease
overview: Polycystic kidney disease is an inherited condition in which clusters of fluid-filled cysts grow in the kidneys, slowly enlarging them and crowding out healthy tissue. It usually runs in families and is often found in adulthood. Many people live full lives for decades with PKD, especially when blood pressure is well controlled. Newer medicines can also slow cyst growth in some people, so regular checkups really pay off.
symptoms: Pain in the back or side
Repeated urinary tract or kidney infections
A feeling of fullness or swelling in the belly

drugs.name: Lisinopril
drugs.note: Controls blood pressure, which helps protect the kidneys.

drugs.name: Losartan
drugs.note: Another first-choice blood pressure medicine for PKD.

drugs.name: Tolvaptan (Jynarque)
drugs.note: Can slow cyst growth in faster-progressing PKD.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Preferred for pain because NSAIDs can stress the kidneys.

redFlags: A sudden, severe "worst of your life" headache needs a 911 call — PKD raises the risk of a brain aneurysm.

name: Acute Kidney Injury
overview: Acute kidney injury is a sudden drop in how well the kidneys filter waste, developing over hours or days. It most often happens to people who are already sick or hospitalized — from dehydration, serious infection, blood loss, or certain medicines. Unlike chronic kidney disease, AKI is often reversible: treating the cause and supporting the body usually lets the kidneys recover, though some people need dialysis for a short time.
symptoms: Making much less urine than usual
Swelling in the legs, ankles, or around the eyes

drugs.name: IV fluids
drugs.note: Restores hydration and blood flow to the kidneys.

drugs.name: Medication review
drugs.note: Doctors pause drugs that stress the kidneys, like NSAIDs.

drugs.name: Furosemide (Lasix)
drugs.note: Helps the body shed extra fluid when it builds up.

drugs.name: Dialysis
drugs.note: Temporarily filters the blood until the kidneys recover.

redFlags: Little or no urine along with swelling, confusion, or trouble breathing is an emergency — go to the ER or call 911.

name: Peripheral Neuropathy
overview: Peripheral neuropathy means the nerves that carry signals between your brain, spinal cord, and the rest of your body are damaged. It often starts as numbness, tingling, or burning in the feet or hands. Diabetes is the most common cause in the U.S., but vitamin shortages, certain medicines, and alcohol can also play a role. Treating the underlying cause can slow or stop the damage, and several medicines help calm nerve pain.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands
Feeling like you're wearing invisible socks or gloves

drugs.name: Gabapentin (Neurontin)
drugs.note: Calms overactive nerve-pain signals.

drugs.name: Pregabalin (Lyrica)
drugs.note: A similar nerve-pain medicine, often used for diabetic neuropathy.

drugs.name: Duloxetine (Cymbalta)
drugs.note: Treats nerve pain even when mood is fine.

drugs.name: Amitriptyline
drugs.note: An older option often taken at bedtime.

drugs.name: Lidocaine or capsaicin patches
drugs.note: Applied to the skin over painful areas.

redFlags: Sudden weakness, numbness that spreads quickly up the body, or loss of bladder or bowel control needs emergency care — call 911 or go to the ER.

resources.label: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

name: Multiple Sclerosis
overview: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks the protective coating around nerves in the brain and spinal cord. That can cause vision problems, numbness, fatigue, and trouble with balance, often in episodes called relapses. MS usually appears between ages 20 and 40 and affects women more often. There's no cure yet, but today's medicines can greatly slow the disease, and many people with MS live full, active lives.
symptoms: Numbness or weakness, often on one side of the body
Blurred or double vision, or pain with eye movement

drugs.name: Ocrelizumab (Ocrevus)
drugs.note: A twice-yearly infusion that slows MS activity.

drugs.name: Glatiramer acetate (Copaxone)
drugs.note: A long-trusted shot that reduces relapses.

drugs.name: Dimethyl fumarate (Tecfidera)
drugs.note: A convenient oral option that lowers relapse risk.

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.note: Short courses help calm a relapse.

redFlags: Sudden vision loss, severe weakness, or trouble speaking should be treated as an emergency — call 911, since a stroke and a severe relapse can look alike.

name: Sciatica
prevalence: about 40% of people at some point in life
overview: Sciatica is pain that travels along the sciatic nerve — from the lower back down through the hip and leg, usually on one side. It most often happens when a slipped (herniated) disk or a bone spur presses on the nerve. The pain can feel sharp, burning, or electric. The good news: most cases get better on their own within weeks with gentle activity, stretching, and over-the-counter pain relievers.
symptoms: Pain radiating from the lower back down one leg
Numbness or tingling in the leg or foot
Pain that worsens with sitting, coughing, or sneezing

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil) / Naproxen (Aleve)
drugs.note: First choice for easing pain and inflammation.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: An option when NSAIDs aren't a good fit.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: Targeted stretches and strengthening speed recovery.

drugs.name: Cyclobenzaprine
drugs.note: Short-term help when back muscles spasm.

drugs.name: Steroid injection
drugs.note: Considered for stubborn pain that won't settle.

redFlags: Loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness in the groin or inner thighs, can signal serious nerve compression — go to the ER right away.

resources.label: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

name: Essential Tremor
overview: Essential tremor is a nervous-system condition that causes rhythmic shaking, most often in the hands — you may notice it when writing, drinking from a cup, or using utensils. It often runs in families and becomes more common with age. It is not Parkinson's disease, though the two are sometimes confused. The tremor isn't dangerous, but it can be frustrating, and medicines — or procedures in tougher cases — can steady things considerably.
symptoms: Shaking of the hands, especially during tasks
Tremor that worsens with stress, caffeine, or tiredness
Shaking that eases when the hands are at rest

drugs.name: Propranolol (Inderal)
drugs.note: The most common first choice for steadying tremor.

drugs.name: Primidone (Mysoline)
drugs.note: Works about as well as propranolol for many people.

drugs.name: Topiramate (Topamax)
drugs.note: A backup when first-line medicines fall short.

drugs.name: Gabapentin (Neurontin)
drugs.note: Sometimes used when other options aren't tolerated.

redFlags: A tremor that starts suddenly, happens at rest, or comes with weakness or slurred speech needs urgent evaluation — call 911 if a stroke is suspected.

name: Concussion
overview: A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury caused by a bump, blow, or jolt to the head — or a hit to the body that shakes the brain. It can cause headache, confusion, dizziness, and memory trouble, even without a loss of consciousness. Most people recover fully within days to weeks with rest and a gradual return to normal activities. Protecting the brain from another hit while it heals is the most important step.
symptoms: Headache or a feeling of pressure in the head
Memory trouble around the time of the injury

drugs.name: Rest and gradual return to activity
drugs.note: The cornerstone of concussion recovery.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Usually preferred for headache in the first days.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil)
drugs.note: Often fine later in recovery — check with your clinician first.

redFlags: A worsening headache, repeated vomiting, one pupil larger than the other, seizures, or trouble waking up means call 911 or go to the ER immediately.

name: Restless Legs Syndrome
overview: Restless legs syndrome causes an uncomfortable urge to move your legs, especially in the evening or when lying down — often described as crawling, tugging, or itching deep inside the legs. Moving brings relief, but the feeling returns when you rest, which can make sleep difficult. Low iron, pregnancy, and certain medicines can trigger or worsen it. Lifestyle changes and several medicines work well for most people, so better nights are very possible.
symptoms: A strong urge to move the legs, especially at rest
Crawling, tugging, or itching feelings deep in the legs
Symptoms that get worse in the evening and at night

drugs.name: Gabapentin enacarbil (Horizant)
drugs.note: An FDA-approved first-line option for nightly symptoms.

drugs.name: Pramipexole (Mirapex)
drugs.note: Eases the urge to move the legs.

drugs.name: Ropinirole (Requip)
drugs.note: A similar option taken in the evening.

drugs.name: Iron supplements
drugs.note: Help when blood tests show low iron stores.

redFlags: RLS itself isn't an emergency, but new leg pain with swelling, warmth, or redness could be a blood clot — seek same-day or emergency care.

name: PCOS
prevalence: ~5 million U.S. women of reproductive age
overview: PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) is a hormone condition that can cause irregular periods, extra facial or body hair, acne, and trouble getting pregnant. It's one of the most common reasons for missed periods in younger women, and it raises the chance of type 2 diabetes later on. There's no cure, but birth control pills, other medicines, and steady habits like regular exercise manage symptoms well — and most women with PCOS can still have children.
symptoms: Extra hair on the face or body
Weight gain that's hard to lose

drugs.name: Combined birth control pills
drugs.note: First-line treatment that regulates periods and improves acne and excess hair.

drugs.name: Metformin (Glucophage)
drugs.note: Improves the body's insulin response and can help restore regular cycles.

drugs.name: Spironolactone (Aldactone)
drugs.note: Reduces acne and unwanted hair growth.

drugs.name: Letrozole (Femara)
drugs.note: First-choice pill to help with ovulation when trying to conceive.

redFlags: Sudden, severe pelvic pain — especially with nausea or vomiting — could signal a twisted ovary, so go to the ER right away.

resources.label: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

name: Endometriosis
overview: Endometriosis happens when tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside it — on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or elsewhere in the pelvis. That tissue swells and bleeds with each cycle, causing painful periods, pain during sex, and sometimes trouble conceiving. It often takes years to get diagnosed, so speaking up about severe period pain matters. Pain relievers, hormone treatments, and surgery can all bring real relief.
symptoms: Very painful periods that interfere with daily life
Pain with bowel movements or urination during periods
Heavy periods or spotting between periods

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Usual first step for easing period pain.

drugs.name: Combined birth control pills
drugs.note: Lighten periods and calm endometriosis pain.

drugs.name: Norethindrone
drugs.note: Hormone pill that thins the misplaced tissue to reduce pain.

drugs.name: Elagolix (Orilissa)
drugs.note: For moderate-to-severe pain when other options fall short.

drugs.name: Laparoscopic surgery
drugs.note: Removes endometriosis tissue and can improve fertility.

redFlags: Sudden, severe pelvic pain with fever, vomiting, or fainting needs emergency care — go to the ER.

resources.label: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

name: Uterine Fibroids
prevalence: Up to ~70% of women by age 50
overview: Uterine fibroids are noncancerous growths of muscle in the wall of the uterus. They're extremely common, and many cause no symptoms at all. When they do, the usual problems are heavy or long periods, pelvic pressure, and frequent urination. Fibroids almost never turn into cancer, and they often shrink on their own after menopause. Treatments range from medicines that lighten bleeding to procedures that remove or shrink the fibroids themselves.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases cramping and mild pain.

drugs.name: Hormonal birth control
drugs.note: Lightens heavy periods, though it doesn't shrink fibroids.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid (Lysteda)
drugs.note: Taken only during periods to cut heavy bleeding.

drugs.name: Leuprolide (Lupron)
drugs.note: Shrinks fibroids temporarily, often before surgery.

drugs.name: Myomectomy or fibroid embolization
drugs.note: Removes or shrinks fibroids while keeping the uterus.

redFlags: Soaking through a pad or tampon every hour, or bleeding with dizziness or fainting, is an emergency — go to the ER.

name: Menopause
prevalence: ~1.3 million U.S. women reach menopause each year
overview: Menopause is the natural point when periods stop for good — usually around age 51 in the U.S. The years leading up to it (perimenopause) can bring hot flashes, night sweats, sleep trouble, mood swings, and vaginal dryness as estrogen levels fall. It's a normal life stage, not an illness, but the symptoms are real and treatable. Hormone therapy and other medicines help many women feel like themselves again.

drugs.name: Estrogen / estrogen-progestin therapy
drugs.note: Most effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats.

drugs.name: Vaginal estrogen
drugs.note: Treats dryness and discomfort with very little hormone absorbed.

drugs.name: Paroxetine (Brisdelle)
drugs.note: Non-hormonal option that reduces hot flashes.

drugs.name: Gabapentin
drugs.note: Can ease hot flashes, especially at night.

redFlags: Any vaginal bleeding after menopause isn't normal — seek same-day care to rule out serious causes.

name: Yeast Infection
prevalence: About 3 in 4 women have one at some point
overview: A vaginal yeast infection happens when a fungus that normally lives in small amounts in the vagina (usually Candida) overgrows, causing itching, burning, and a thick white discharge. Antibiotics, pregnancy, and diabetes can make one more likely. Yeast infections are very common, not a sign of poor hygiene, and not usually spread through sex. Over-the-counter creams or a single prescription pill clear most infections within a few days.
symptoms: Redness and swelling of the vulva

drugs.name: Miconazole (Monistat)
drugs.note: Over-the-counter cream or suppository used for one to seven days.

drugs.name: Fluconazole (Diflucan)
drugs.note: Single prescription pill that clears most infections.

drugs.name: Clotrimazole
drugs.note: Another over-the-counter cream option.

drugs.name: Terconazole
drugs.note: Prescription cream for stubborn infections.

redFlags: If you also have fever, chills, or pelvic pain, it may be a more serious infection — seek same-day care.

name: PMS & PMDD
prevalence: PMS affects ~3 in 4 menstruating women; PMDD about 5%
overview: PMS is the cluster of symptoms — bloating, breast tenderness, irritability, food cravings — that shows up in the week or two before a period and fades once it starts. PMDD is a more severe form in which mood symptoms like depression, anger, or anxiety seriously disrupt daily life. Both are common and very treatable. Tracking your symptoms across a couple of cycles helps your doctor confirm the pattern and find the right treatment.
symptoms: With PMDD: intense sadness, anger, or anxiety
Symptoms lift within days of the period starting

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases cramps, headaches, and breast tenderness.

drugs.name: Sertraline (Zoloft) / Fluoxetine (Prozac)
drugs.note: First-choice medicines for PMDD mood symptoms.

drugs.name: Drospirenone birth control (Yaz)
drugs.note: Birth control pill that is FDA-approved for PMDD.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.note: Can reduce bloating and breast tenderness.

redFlags: If premenstrual mood symptoms ever include thoughts of self-harm or suicide, call or text 988 or go to the ER.

name: Cervical Cancer
overview: Cervical cancer starts in the cervix, the lower part of the uterus, and is almost always caused by long-lasting infection with HPV, a very common virus. It grows slowly, which is why it's one of the most preventable cancers: the HPV vaccine prevents most cases, and routine Pap and HPV tests can catch cell changes years before cancer ever develops. Found early, cervical cancer is highly treatable, often with surgery alone.
symptoms: Bleeding between periods or after sex
Pelvic pain or pain during sex

drugs.name: Surgery (cone biopsy or hysterectomy)
drugs.note: Main treatment for early-stage cancer.

drugs.name: Radiation therapy
drugs.note: Often combined with chemo for larger tumors.

drugs.name: Cisplatin
drugs.note: Most common chemo, usually given alongside radiation.

drugs.name: HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9)
drugs.note: Prevents the infections that cause most cervical cancers.

redFlags: Heavy vaginal bleeding with dizziness, fainting, or a racing heartbeat is an emergency — call 911 or go to the ER.

name: Ovarian Cysts
prevalence: About 8% of premenopausal women develop one needing treatment
overview: Ovarian cysts are fluid-filled sacs that form on or inside an ovary, usually as a normal part of the monthly cycle. Most cause no symptoms, are found by chance on an ultrasound, and go away on their own within a few months. Some cause a pelvic ache, bloating, or pain during sex. Cysts are almost always benign, especially before menopause, so doctors often simply monitor them and treat pain if needed.
symptoms: Dull pelvic ache or pressure on one side
Bloating or a feeling of fullness
Sudden sharp pain if a cyst ruptures or twists

drugs.name: Watchful waiting
drugs.note: Most cysts go away on their own within a few months.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Relieves pelvic ache while a cyst resolves.

drugs.name: Hormonal birth control
drugs.note: Helps prevent new cysts from forming.

drugs.name: Laparoscopic surgery
drugs.note: Removes large or persistent cysts through tiny incisions.

redFlags: Sudden, sharp pelvic pain with fever, vomiting, or faintness can mean a ruptured or twisted cyst — go to the ER.

resources.label: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

name: Pancreatic Cancer
overview: Pancreatic cancer starts in the pancreas, an organ behind the stomach that makes digestive juices and insulin. Because early symptoms are vague, it is often found after it has spread, which makes it one of the harder cancers to treat. When caught early, surgery can remove it, and chemotherapy helps at every stage. Researchers are working hard on better tests and treatments, and care teams can do a lot to ease symptoms.
symptoms: Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
Belly pain that spreads to the back

drugs.name: FOLFIRINOX
drugs.note: A mix of chemo medicines often used for people healthy enough to handle it.

drugs.name: Gemcitabine (Gemzar)
drugs.note: A long-standing mainstay, used alone or in combinations.

drugs.name: Nab-paclitaxel (Abraxane)
drugs.note: Often paired with gemcitabine.

drugs.name: Whipple surgery
drugs.note: Removes the tumor when the cancer is caught early enough.

redFlags: New yellowing of the skin or eyes, severe belly pain, or vomiting that won't stop needs same-day medical care.

name: Leukemia
aka: Cancer of the blood and bone marrow
overview: Leukemia is cancer of the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. It crowds out healthy blood cells, leading to fatigue, infections, and easy bruising. There are several types — acute kinds come on fast, while chronic kinds grow slowly, sometimes for years. Treatment has improved dramatically: some forms are highly curable, especially in children, and others can be controlled for the long term with a daily pill.

drugs.name: Cytarabine
drugs.note: A backbone chemo medicine for acute leukemia.

drugs.name: Imatinib (Gleevec)
drugs.note: A daily pill that transformed treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia.

drugs.name: Ibrutinib (Imbruvica)
drugs.note: A pill commonly used for chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

drugs.name: Rituximab (Rituxan)
drugs.note: Often combined with other medicines for certain types.

redFlags: A high fever, bleeding that won't stop, or sudden trouble breathing needs emergency care — call 911 or go to the ER.

name: Lymphoma
overview: Lymphoma is cancer of the lymphatic system — the network of nodes and vessels that helps your body fight infection. The two main families are Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and the first sign is often a painless swollen lymph node in the neck, armpit, or groin. Many lymphomas respond very well to treatment, and Hodgkin lymphoma is one of the most curable cancers, even when found at a later stage.

drugs.name: Rituximab (Rituxan)
drugs.note: A mainstay for most non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

drugs.name: R-CHOP
drugs.note: The standard first treatment for many non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

drugs.name: ABVD
drugs.note: A common first treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma.

drugs.name: Radiation therapy
drugs.note: Targets specific groups of affected lymph nodes.

redFlags: A rapidly growing lump with trouble breathing or swallowing, or a fever with shaking chills, needs emergency care — go to the ER.

name: Bladder Cancer
overview: Bladder cancer starts in the lining of the bladder, and its most common warning sign is blood in the urine. Smoking is the biggest risk factor. The good news: most cases are found early, while the cancer is still in the bladder's inner layer, where it is very treatable and often curable. Because bladder cancer can come back, regular checkups with a urologist are a key part of care.
symptoms: Needing to urinate more often than usual
Feeling a sudden, strong urge to go
Lower back pain on one side

drugs.name: TURBT surgery
drugs.note: Removes bladder tumors through the urethra — no incision needed.

drugs.name: BCG therapy
drugs.note: Placed directly into the bladder to keep early cancer from returning.

drugs.name: Mitomycin
drugs.note: Another medicine placed inside the bladder after tumor removal.

drugs.name: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy
drugs.note: Used when cancer grows into the bladder muscle.

redFlags: Heavy bleeding with clots or being unable to pass urine at all is an emergency — go to the ER.

name: Kidney Cancer
overview: Most kidney cancers are renal cell carcinoma, which starts in the tiny tubes that filter your blood. Many cases today are found early — often by accident on a scan done for something else — and surgery alone frequently cures those. For cancer that has spread, newer immunotherapy and targeted pills have greatly improved the outlook compared with a decade ago, and treatment keeps getting better.
symptoms: A lump or pain in the side or lower back

drugs.name: Kidney surgery (nephrectomy)
drugs.note: Removing part or all of the kidney often cures early kidney cancer.

drugs.name: Pembrolizumab (Keytruda)
drugs.note: Helps the immune system find and attack cancer cells.

drugs.name: Cabozantinib (Cabometyx)
drugs.note: A pill that blocks signals tumors use to grow.

drugs.name: Nivolumab (Opdivo)
drugs.note: Another immune-boosting option, sometimes used in combinations.

redFlags: Heavy or persistent blood in the urine, or severe one-sided back pain with fever, needs same-day medical care.

name: Ovarian Cancer
overview: Ovarian cancer begins in the ovaries or fallopian tubes. Its early symptoms — bloating, pelvic pain, feeling full quickly — are easy to mistake for everyday stomach issues, so it is often found at a later stage. Treatment usually combines surgery with chemotherapy, and newer maintenance pills help keep the cancer from coming back. Women with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer should ask their doctor about genetic testing.
symptoms: Needing to urinate urgently or often
Bleeding after menopause or unusual periods

drugs.name: Carboplatin
drugs.note: The backbone chemo medicine for ovarian cancer.

drugs.name: Paclitaxel (Taxol)
drugs.note: Usually given together with carboplatin.

drugs.name: Debulking surgery
drugs.note: Removes as much of the cancer as possible.

drugs.name: Olaparib (Lynparza)
drugs.note: A maintenance pill that helps keep cancer from returning.

redFlags: Severe belly pain with vomiting, a hard swollen abdomen, or trouble breathing needs emergency care — go to the ER.

resources.label: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

name: Glaucoma
overview: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve — the cable carrying images from your eye to your brain — usually because of high pressure inside the eye. It develops slowly and silently, often stealing side vision first, so many people don't notice until damage is done. There's no cure, but daily eye drops, laser treatment, or surgery can lower eye pressure and protect the vision you still have. Regular eye exams catch it early.
symptoms: In sudden attacks: severe eye pain, halos around lights, and nausea

drugs.name: Latanoprost (Xalatan)
drugs.note: First-choice nightly drop that lowers eye pressure.

drugs.name: Timolol (Timoptic)
drugs.note: Cuts down the amount of fluid the eye makes.

drugs.name: Brimonidine (Alphagan P)
drugs.note: Often added when one drop isn't enough.

drugs.name: Dorzolamide (Trusopt)
drugs.note: Another add-on that lowers fluid production.

drugs.name: Laser trabeculoplasty
drugs.note: Quick office laser that helps fluid drain from the eye.

redFlags: Sudden severe eye pain with blurred vision, halos around lights, headache, or nausea can be an acute glaucoma attack — go to the ER right away.

name: Cataracts
overview: A cataract is a clouding of the eye's natural lens, like looking through a foggy window. It's a normal part of aging — most people develop some clouding as they get older. Vision slowly gets blurry, colors fade, and glare at night gets worse. The good news: cataract surgery is one of the safest and most common operations in the U.S., replacing the cloudy lens with a clear artificial one and restoring sharp vision for most people.
symptoms: Colors that look faded or yellowed
Glare and halos, especially driving at night

drugs.name: Cataract surgery
drugs.note: Replaces the cloudy lens with a clear artificial one; the only real fix.

drugs.name: Updated glasses or contacts
drugs.note: A stronger prescription and anti-glare coating help in early stages.

drugs.name: Brighter lighting and magnifiers
drugs.note: Simple home changes that ease reading until surgery is needed.

redFlags: Sudden vision loss, flashes of light, or a dark curtain over your vision is not a cataract — seek same-day eye care.

name: Macular Degeneration
overview: Macular degeneration affects the macula — the small center of the retina you use for reading, driving, and recognizing faces. It blurs central vision while side vision stays intact, so it does not cause total blindness. The common 'dry' form usually progresses slowly; the 'wet' form moves faster but can be treated with eye injections that often save sight. Special vitamin formulas can slow the disease in some people, which is why early detection matters.
symptoms: Straight lines that look wavy or bent
A dark or empty spot in the middle of your view

drugs.name: AREDS2 vitamins
drugs.note: A specific vitamin formula that slows dry AMD in some people.

drugs.name: Aflibercept (Eylea)
drugs.note: In-office eye injection that treats wet AMD.

drugs.name: Ranibizumab (Lucentis)
drugs.note: Another commonly used injection for wet AMD.

drugs.name: Bevacizumab (Avastin)
drugs.note: A lower-cost option used the same way.

redFlags: If straight lines suddenly look wavy or a dark spot appears in your central vision, get same-day care from an eye doctor — wet AMD can damage sight quickly.

name: Dry Eye
overview: Dry eye happens when your eyes don't make enough tears, or the tears dry up too fast. It causes burning, grittiness, and — surprisingly — watery eyes, since irritation triggers reflex tearing. Screen time, aging, dry air, contact lenses, and some medicines all make it worse. It's uncomfortable but rarely serious, and most people get real relief with artificial tears, warm compresses, and small habit changes like taking regular screen breaks.
symptoms: Blurry vision that clears when you blink
Tired eyes after reading or screen use

drugs.name: Artificial tears (OTC)
drugs.note: The first step; can be used as often as needed.

drugs.name: Lubricating gel or ointment
drugs.note: Thicker overnight relief for eyes that dry out while you sleep.

drugs.name: Cyclosporine (Restasis)
drugs.note: Prescription drop that helps your eyes make more of their own tears.

drugs.name: Lifitegrast (Xiidra)
drugs.note: An alternative prescription for stubborn cases.

redFlags: Severe eye pain, light sensitivity, or a sudden change in vision is more than dry eye — seek same-day eye care.

name: Pink Eye (Conjunctivitis)
overview: Pink eye is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the clear film covering the white of the eye. Viruses cause most cases, and those clear up on their own in a week or two; bacteria and allergies cause the rest. It spreads easily, so wash your hands often and don't share towels or pillowcases. Most pink eye looks worse than it is and doesn't harm vision, but a doctor can tell which kind you have and whether drops will help.
symptoms: Pink or red color in the white of the eye
Itching, burning, or a gritty feeling
Crusty lashes, especially in the morning

drugs.name: Artificial tears and cool compresses
drugs.note: Soothe most viral cases while they run their course.

drugs.name: Polymyxin B / trimethoprim (Polytrim)
drugs.note: Used when a doctor confirms bacterial pink eye.

drugs.name: Erythromycin ointment
drugs.note: A common bacterial option, especially for kids.

drugs.name: Ketotifen (Zaditor)
drugs.note: Calms itchy, allergy-driven pink eye.

redFlags: Eye pain, blurred vision, intense redness, severe light sensitivity, or pink eye in a newborn needs same-day medical care.

name: Diabetic Retinopathy
overview: Diabetic retinopathy is eye damage caused by high blood sugar weakening the tiny blood vessels in the retina. It's a leading cause of new blindness in working-age American adults — yet it often has no early symptoms at all. That's why everyone with diabetes needs a dilated eye exam every year. Keeping blood sugar and blood pressure in range slows the damage, and modern treatments like eye injections protect vision when it's caught in time.
symptoms: Floaters (dark spots or strings drifting in view)
Dark or empty areas in your vision

drugs.name: Blood sugar and blood pressure control
drugs.note: The foundation of treatment — it slows damage at every stage.

drugs.name: Aflibercept (Eylea)
drugs.note: Eye injection that treats swelling and abnormal blood vessels.

drugs.name: Ranibizumab (Lucentis)
drugs.note: Another widely used injection for diabetic eye disease.

drugs.name: Laser photocoagulation
drugs.note: Seals leaking vessels in more advanced disease.

redFlags: A sudden shower of floaters, flashes of light, or a dark curtain over your vision can signal bleeding or retinal detachment — get emergency eye care the same day.

name: Low Back Pain
