prevalence: About 8 in 10 U.S. adults at some point in life
overview: Low back pain is one of the most common reasons people see a doctor — most adults will deal with it at some point. It usually comes from strained muscles, ligaments, or normal wear in the spine, not from anything dangerous. The good news: most episodes get better within a few weeks with gentle movement, over-the-counter pain relievers, and time. Staying active actually helps you heal faster than bed rest.
symptoms: Aching or stiffness in the lower back
Pain that worsens with bending or lifting
Pain that sometimes shoots down a leg (sciatica)

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: First choice for easing pain and inflammation.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: An option when NSAIDs aren't a good fit.

drugs.name: Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)
drugs.note: Short-term help for painful muscle spasms.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: Builds strength and helps prevent repeat episodes.

redFlags: Back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin, or leg weakness can signal serious nerve compression — go to the ER.

name: Neck Pain
prevalence: About 1 in 3 U.S. adults each year
overview: Neck pain is extremely common and usually comes from muscle strain — think long hours at a desk, sleeping in an awkward position, or stress that tightens the shoulders. Most cases ease up within days to a few weeks with gentle stretching, heat, and over-the-counter pain relievers. Less often, a pinched nerve causes pain that travels down the arm; that usually improves too, but takes longer.
symptoms: Stiff, sore neck that's hard to turn
Headaches that start at the base of the skull
Pain that worsens after sitting or driving
Tingling that travels into the shoulder or arm

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain and calms inflammation.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: A gentler option for mild pain.

drugs.name: Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)
drugs.note: Used briefly for muscle spasms.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: Stretching and strengthening for lasting relief.

redFlags: Neck pain after a car crash or fall, or pain with fever and a stiff neck, or new arm weakness or numbness, needs emergency care — go to the ER.

name: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
overview: Carpal tunnel syndrome happens when the median nerve gets squeezed as it passes through a narrow tunnel in your wrist, causing numbness, tingling, and weakness in the hand — often worse at night. Typing, assembly work, and conditions like diabetes or pregnancy can raise the risk. Caught early, it often improves with a simple wrist splint; when it doesn't, a brief outpatient surgery brings relief for most people.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling in the thumb and first fingers
Symptoms that wake you up at night
A 'pins and needles' feeling when gripping
Relief from shaking out the hand

drugs.name: Wrist splint
drugs.note: Worn at night to keep the wrist straight.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: May ease pain, though relief is often modest.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: Reduces swelling around the nerve.

drugs.name: Carpal tunnel release
drugs.note: A short outpatient surgery that relieves the pressure.

redFlags: Constant numbness, a weakening grip, or shrinking muscle at the base of the thumb can mean lasting nerve damage — seek same-day care.

name: Plantar Fasciitis
overview: Plantar fasciitis is irritation of the thick band of tissue (the plantar fascia) that runs along the bottom of your foot, causing stabbing heel pain — classically with the first steps in the morning. Runners, people who stand all day, and those carrying extra weight get it most. It's stubborn but rarely serious: stretching, supportive shoes, and time resolve most cases within several months.
symptoms: Stabbing heel pain with the first steps of the day
Tenderness at the bottom of the heel
Pain after long periods of standing
Stiffness that eases as you move

drugs.name: Stretching exercises
drugs.note: Daily calf and foot stretches are the core treatment.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Takes the edge off heel pain.

drugs.name: Orthotic shoe inserts
drugs.note: Cushion the heel and support the arch.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: For stubborn pain that won't settle.

redFlags: A sudden pop with severe heel pain or being unable to put weight on the foot could mean a rupture or fracture — seek same-day care.

name: Rotator Cuff Injury
prevalence: ~2 million U.S. doctor visits each year
overview: Your rotator cuff is the group of muscles and tendons that keeps your shoulder stable and lets you raise your arm. Injuries range from inflammation and small fraying to full tears, and they're very common with age — many tears come from normal wear, not accidents. Pain often shows up when reaching overhead or lying on the sore side. Most people improve with physical therapy and don't need surgery.
symptoms: Dull ache deep in the shoulder
Pain when reaching overhead or behind the back
Pain at night, especially lying on that side

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain and swelling.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: The mainstay — restores strength and motion.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: Can calm pain enough to make therapy easier.

drugs.name: Rotator cuff repair
drugs.note: Surgery for full tears or pain that won't improve.

redFlags: If you can't lift your arm at all after a fall or sudden injury, the tendon may be fully torn — seek same-day care.

name: Knee Injuries (ACL & Meniscus)
prevalence: ~200,000 ACL injuries in the U.S. each year
overview: The ACL is a ligament that keeps the knee stable, and the meniscus is the cartilage cushion inside it — both are commonly injured in sports that involve pivoting, jumping, or sudden stops. A pop, swelling, and a knee that feels wobbly are classic signs. Some tears heal with physical therapy alone; others, especially ACL tears in active people, are repaired with a well-established outpatient surgery followed by months of rehab.
symptoms: A 'pop' felt or heard at the moment of injury
A knee that buckles or feels unstable

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain and swelling after injury.

drugs.name: RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation)
drugs.note: First aid in the days after injury.

drugs.name: Physical therapy
drugs.note: Rebuilds strength and stability.

drugs.name: Arthroscopic surgery
drugs.note: Repairs or reconstructs tears through small incisions.

redFlags: A knee that looks deformed, won't bear any weight, or comes with a numb or cold foot needs emergency care — go to the ER.

name: Tendinitis
prevalence: Affects millions of Americans each year
overview: Tendinitis is irritation or inflammation of a tendon — the strong cord that attaches muscle to bone. It usually comes from repeating the same motion over and over, which is why names like tennis elbow, golfer's elbow, and jumper's knee are so familiar. The fix is rarely complicated: rest the area, ice it, ease the pain with over-the-counter medicine, and return to activity gradually.
symptoms: Dull ache where the tendon meets the bone
Tenderness when pressing on the area
Pain that worsens with the repeated motion

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: First-line relief for pain and inflammation.

drugs.name: Diclofenac gel (Voltaren)
drugs.note: Rubbed on the skin right where it hurts.

drugs.name: Rest and ice
drugs.note: Gives the tendon time to settle down.

drugs.name: Corticosteroid injection
drugs.note: For pain that doesn't improve — used sparingly.

redFlags: A sudden snap or pop followed by weakness or inability to move the joint may mean the tendon has ruptured — seek same-day care.

name: Common Cold
prevalence: About 1 billion colds in the U.S. each year
overview: The common cold is a mild viral infection of the nose and throat, most often caused by rhinoviruses. Adults catch two to three colds a year on average, and kids get even more. There's no cure — antibiotics don't work on viruses — but rest, fluids, and over-the-counter remedies ease symptoms while your body clears the infection, usually within 7 to 10 days.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases aches and lowers fever.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another option for aches and fever.

drugs.name: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed)
drugs.note: Helps unblock a stuffy nose for short stretches.

drugs.name: Dextromethorphan (Delsym, Robitussin)
drugs.note: Quiets a dry, nagging cough.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fever that lasts more than a few days means it may be more than a cold — seek same-day care.

name: Flu (Influenza)
prevalence: Roughly 10–40 million U.S. illnesses each flu season
overview: Influenza is a contagious respiratory virus that hits harder and faster than a cold — fever, body aches, and exhaustion often arrive within a day. Most healthy people recover in one to two weeks, but flu can be serious for older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with chronic health conditions. A yearly flu shot is the best protection, and antiviral pills can shorten the illness if started early.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases fever and body aches.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another option for fever and aches.

drugs.name: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu)
drugs.note: Can shorten the flu if started within the first 48 hours.

drugs.name: Baloxavir (Xofluza)
drugs.note: Single-dose alternative for early treatment.

drugs.name: Annual flu vaccine
drugs.note: The best way to prevent flu in the first place.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, bluish lips, or signs of serious dehydration mean go to the ER or call 911.

name: Strep Throat
prevalence: Several million U.S. cases each year
overview: Strep throat is a bacterial infection of the throat and tonsils caused by group A streptococcus. Unlike most sore throats, which are viral, strep needs antibiotics — both to speed recovery and to prevent rare complications like rheumatic fever. It spreads easily through coughs and sneezes, especially among school-age kids. A quick swab test at the doctor's office confirms it, and most people feel better within a day or two of starting treatment.
symptoms: Sore throat that comes on fast
Red, swollen tonsils, sometimes with white patches
Swollen, tender glands in the neck

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.note: A common first choice, especially for kids.

drugs.name: Penicillin
drugs.note: The classic, reliable first-line treatment.

drugs.name: Cephalexin (Keflex)
drugs.note: An option for some people with penicillin allergy.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases throat pain and fever while antibiotics work.

redFlags: Trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, or severe neck swelling needs emergency care right away.

resources.label: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

name: Acute Bronchitis
prevalence: About 1 in 20 U.S. adults each year
overview: Acute bronchitis — often called a chest cold — happens when the airways in your lungs get inflamed, usually after a viral infection like a cold or the flu. The main symptom is a nagging cough that can hang around for up to three weeks, sometimes with mucus. Because viruses cause most cases, antibiotics usually don't help. Rest, fluids, honey, and over-the-counter remedies are the mainstays while your airways heal on their own.
symptoms: Cough lasting up to three weeks
Mucus that may be clear, yellow, or green

drugs.name: Dextromethorphan (Delsym, Robitussin)
drugs.note: Calms the cough so you can rest.

drugs.name: Guaifenesin (Mucinex)
drugs.note: Thins mucus so it's easier to cough up.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases chest soreness and any fever.

drugs.name: Albuterol (Ventolin)
drugs.note: Sometimes prescribed when there's wheezing.

redFlags: Coughing up blood, a high fever, or shortness of breath at rest are reasons to seek same-day care — and severe trouble breathing means call 911.

name: Mono (Mononucleosis)
prevalence: About 1 in 4 U.S. teens and young adults who catch EBV develop mono
overview: Mono is a viral illness, usually caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, that spreads through saliva — which earned it the nickname 'the kissing disease.' It's most common in teens and young adults, bringing weeks of deep fatigue, sore throat, and swollen glands. There's no specific cure; rest, fluids, and time are the main treatment. Most people recover fully, though the tiredness can linger for a month or more.
symptoms: Swollen glands in the neck and armpits

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases fever and sore throat.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another option for aches and swelling.

drugs.name: Rest and fluids
drugs.note: The real treatment — mono simply takes time.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: Occasionally used if throat swelling makes breathing or swallowing hard.

redFlags: Sudden, sharp pain in the upper-left belly could mean a ruptured spleen — go to the ER immediately.

resources.label: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

name: Stomach Flu (Gastroenteritis)
prevalence: About 20 million U.S. norovirus illnesses alone each year
overview: Stomach flu isn't actually the flu — it's an infection of the stomach and intestines, most often caused by viruses like norovirus. It brings sudden vomiting, diarrhea, and cramps that usually clear up on their own within one to three days. The biggest risk is dehydration, so sipping fluids is the most important treatment. It spreads very easily, so good handwashing protects the rest of the household.

drugs.name: Oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte)
drugs.note: Replaces the fluids and salts lost to vomiting and diarrhea.

drugs.name: Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol)
drugs.note: Can ease nausea and diarrhea in adults.

drugs.name: Loperamide (Imodium)
drugs.note: Slows diarrhea — skip it if there's blood or a high fever.

drugs.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
drugs.note: Prescription option when vomiting won't let up.

redFlags: Signs of serious dehydration — little or no urination, dizziness, confusion — or blood in vomit or stool mean go to the ER.

name: Constipation
overview: Constipation means bowel movements that are infrequent, hard, or difficult to pass — and nearly everyone deals with it at some point. It's usually caused by too little fiber or fluid, inactivity, certain medicines, or simply ignoring the urge to go. It's rarely a sign of something serious, and most cases improve with more fiber, more water, regular movement, and gentle over-the-counter laxatives when needed.
symptoms: Fewer than three bowel movements a week
Feeling like you can't fully empty

drugs.name: Polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX)
drugs.note: Gentle option that draws water into the stool.

drugs.name: Psyllium (Metamucil)
drugs.note: Bulk-forming fiber that keeps things moving.

drugs.name: Docusate (Colace)
drugs.note: Makes stool easier to pass.

drugs.name: Senna (Senokot)
drugs.note: For short-term use when gentler options aren't enough.

redFlags: Severe belly pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen, or being unable to pass gas or stool at all could signal a blockage — go to the ER.

name: Hemorrhoids
prevalence: About 1 in 20 Americans, and about half of adults over 50
overview: Hemorrhoids are swollen veins in or around the anus — a very common and very treatable problem. Straining during bowel movements, chronic constipation, pregnancy, and long stretches of sitting all raise the risk. They can itch, hurt, or bleed a little during bowel movements, which is alarming but rarely dangerous. Most improve with fiber, fluids, warm sitz baths, and over-the-counter creams, and stubborn ones can be handled with simple office procedures.
symptoms: Itching or irritation around the anus
Pain or discomfort, especially when sitting
Small amounts of bright red blood with bowel movements
Swelling or a tender lump near the anus

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone cream (Anusol-HC)
drugs.note: Calms itching and swelling for short-term use.

drugs.name: Phenylephrine ointment (Preparation H)
drugs.note: Shrinks swollen tissue and eases discomfort.

drugs.name: Witch hazel pads (Tucks)
drugs.note: Cools and gently cleans the area.

drugs.name: Psyllium (Metamucil)
drugs.note: Softens stool so there's less straining.

drugs.name: Warm sitz baths
drugs.note: Soaking eases pain and helps healing.

redFlags: Heavy rectal bleeding or bleeding with dizziness or lightheadedness needs emergency care, and any new rectal bleeding deserves a doctor's check to rule out other causes.

name: Vitamin D Deficiency
prevalence: Roughly 1 in 4 Americans have low levels
overview: Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium and keep bones strong, and your skin makes it from sunlight. Many Americans run low — especially during winter, with darker skin tones, or with limited time outdoors. Mild deficiency usually causes no symptoms and shows up only on a blood test, but over time low vitamin D can weaken bones and muscles. The fix is usually straightforward: an inexpensive daily supplement brings most people back to normal.

drugs.name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
drugs.note: The standard over-the-counter daily supplement.

drugs.name: Vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol)
drugs.note: Higher-strength option doctors prescribe for bigger shortfalls.

drugs.name: Calcium with vitamin D
drugs.note: Often paired together for bone health.

drugs.name: Sunlight and diet
drugs.note: Short stretches of sun plus fatty fish and fortified foods help.

redFlags: Low vitamin D itself is rarely an emergency, but sudden severe bone pain or a suspected fracture needs same-day care.

name: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
prevalence: About 6 in 100 U.S. adults under 60, more with age
overview: Vitamin B12 keeps your nerves and blood cells healthy, and your body gets it from animal foods like meat, eggs, and dairy. Deficiency creeps up slowly — causing fatigue, numbness, and memory trouble — and is more common in older adults, vegans, and people taking certain stomach-acid or diabetes medicines. Caught early, it's very treatable with supplements or shots, but long-untreated deficiency can cause lasting nerve damage.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling in hands and feet

drugs.name: Cyanocobalamin tablets
drugs.note: Daily over-the-counter pills work for most people.

drugs.name: Cyanocobalamin injections
drugs.note: Used when the body can't absorb B12 from food.

drugs.name: Cyanocobalamin nasal spray (Nascobal)
drugs.note: A needle-free option once levels are stable.

drugs.name: B12-rich foods
drugs.note: More meat, fish, eggs, dairy, or fortified foods.

redFlags: New numbness, trouble walking, or confusion needs same-day evaluation — untreated B12 deficiency can cause permanent nerve damage.

name: Bipolar Disorder
overview: Bipolar disorder causes unusual shifts in mood and energy — periods of feeling extremely "up" (mania) and periods of deep depression. These swings go far beyond everyday ups and downs and can disrupt work, sleep, and relationships. It usually starts in the late teens or early adult years. With mood-stabilizing medicine and therapy, most people can even out the swings and live full, productive lives.
symptoms: Periods of high energy, racing thoughts, and little need for sleep
Risky or impulsive behavior during "up" periods
Stretches of deep sadness or hopelessness
Big swings in energy and activity
Trouble keeping up at work or school during episodes

drugs.name: Lithium
drugs.note: The classic, well-proven medicine for evening out mood swings.

drugs.name: Quetiapine (Seroquel)
drugs.note: Treats both the manic and depressive sides.

drugs.name: Lamotrigine (Lamictal)
drugs.note: Especially helpful at preventing the depressive lows.

drugs.name: Valproate (Depakote)
drugs.note: Often used to calm acute mania.

drugs.name: Aripiprazole (Abilify)
drugs.note: Helps control mania and prevent future episodes.

redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, or mania so severe that someone may hurt themselves, are emergencies — call or text 988, or call 911 if there is immediate danger.

name: PTSD
prevalence: ~12 million U.S. adults in a given year
overview: PTSD can develop after living through or witnessing something terrifying — combat, an assault, an accident, or a disaster. The brain's alarm system stays stuck on "high alert," bringing nightmares, flashbacks, and a constant feeling of being on edge. It is not a sign of weakness, and it can affect anyone. Trauma-focused therapy works well for most people, and certain antidepressants can help too.
symptoms: Flashbacks or nightmares that replay the event
Avoiding places, people, or reminders of what happened
Feeling jumpy, on edge, or easily startled
Feeling numb, guilty, or detached from others

drugs.name: Trauma-focused therapy
drugs.note: The most effective treatment — helps the brain process the trauma safely.

drugs.name: Sertraline (Zoloft)
drugs.note: FDA-approved for PTSD; eases anxiety and low mood.

drugs.name: Paroxetine (Paxil)
drugs.note: The other FDA-approved medicine for PTSD.

drugs.name: Prazosin
drugs.note: Sometimes used to quiet trauma-related nightmares.

redFlags: If thoughts of suicide or self-harm appear, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline right away, or call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

name: OCD
overview: OCD causes unwanted, intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repeated behaviors a person feels driven to do (compulsions), like excessive hand-washing or checking. People with OCD usually know the thoughts don't make sense, but the urge to act on them is powerful and time-consuming. It's a brain-based condition — not a personality quirk — and a specific type of therapy plus medication brings real relief to most people.
symptoms: Unwanted thoughts or fears that keep coming back
Repeated rituals like washing, checking, or counting
Rituals that eat up an hour or more each day

drugs.name: Exposure & response prevention (ERP)
drugs.note: The gold-standard therapy that retrains the brain's alarm response.

drugs.name: Sertraline (Zoloft)
drugs.note: A first-choice medicine, often at higher strengths than for depression.

drugs.name: Fluoxetine (Prozac)
drugs.note: Another common first-line option for OCD.

drugs.name: Clomipramine (Anafranil)
drugs.note: An older medicine used when SSRIs don't help enough.

redFlags: If intrusive thoughts turn toward suicide or self-harm, call or text 988 right away, and seek same-day care if symptoms suddenly make daily life impossible.

name: Panic Disorder
overview: Panic disorder causes sudden waves of intense fear — panic attacks — that can strike out of the blue, with a racing heart, shortness of breath, dizziness, and a feeling that something terrible is happening. Attacks usually peak within minutes and pass, but the fear of the next one can start to take over daily life. The good news: panic disorder is one of the most treatable anxiety conditions.
symptoms: Sudden surges of intense fear or dread
Shortness of breath or chest tightness
Worry about when the next attack will hit
Avoiding places where attacks have happened

drugs.name: Sertraline (Zoloft)
drugs.note: A first-choice daily medicine that makes attacks less frequent.

drugs.name: Escitalopram (Lexapro)
drugs.note: Another common first-line daily option.

drugs.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy
drugs.note: Teaches skills that take the power out of panic attacks.

drugs.name: Alprazolam (Xanax)
drugs.note: Short-term rescue for severe attacks; can be habit-forming.

redFlags: A first-time attack with chest pain or trouble breathing can mimic a heart attack — call 911 to be safe — and call or text 988 for any thoughts of self-harm.

name: Schizophrenia
overview: Schizophrenia is a serious brain disorder that changes how a person thinks, feels, and perceives reality. It can cause hallucinations (hearing or seeing things others don't), fixed false beliefs, and trouble organizing thoughts. Symptoms usually appear between the late teens and early 30s. It is not "split personality," and it is no one's fault. Antipsychotic medicine plus steady support helps many people manage symptoms and live meaningful lives.
symptoms: Hearing voices or seeing things others don't
Strong beliefs that don't match reality
Jumbled thoughts or speech that's hard to follow
Pulling away from friends and family
Loss of motivation or emotional expression

drugs.name: Risperidone (Risperdal)
drugs.note: A common first-choice medicine for easing hallucinations and delusions.

drugs.name: Aripiprazole (Abilify)
drugs.note: A first-line option that tends to cause less weight gain.

drugs.name: Olanzapine (Zyprexa)
drugs.note: Effective, though it can affect weight and blood sugar.

drugs.name: Clozapine (Clozaril)
drugs.note: Reserved for when other medicines haven't worked; needs blood monitoring.

redFlags: If someone may harm themselves or others, or voices are commanding them to, call 911 or call/text 988 immediately.

name: Alcohol Use Disorder
overview: Alcohol use disorder means drinking has become hard to control and keeps causing problems — at home, at work, or with health — yet stopping feels difficult. It ranges from mild to severe, and it is a medical condition, not a moral failing. Effective treatments exist, including medications that reduce cravings, counseling, and support groups, and many people recover fully. Even cutting back brings real health benefits.
symptoms: Drinking more, or longer, than intended
Needing more drinks to feel the same effect
Drinking despite problems with family, work, or health
Shakiness, sweating, or nausea when not drinking

drugs.name: Naltrexone (Vivitrol)
drugs.note: A first-choice medicine that dulls the urge to drink.

drugs.name: Acamprosate (Campral)
drugs.note: Helps the brain stay steady after quitting.

drugs.name: Counseling & support groups
drugs.note: Therapy and groups like AA are a core part of recovery.

drugs.name: Disulfiram (Antabuse)
drugs.note: Causes unpleasant effects if alcohol is consumed.

redFlags: Withdrawal with confusion, seizures, or hallucinations after heavy drinking stops is life-threatening — call 911 — and call or text 988 for thoughts of self-harm.

resources.label: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism

name: Eating Disorders
prevalence: about 9% of Americans in their lifetime
overview: Eating disorders — including anorexia, bulimia, and binge-eating disorder — are serious conditions in which eating, weight, and body image take over a person's thoughts and health. They affect people of every gender, age, and body size, and they are medical illnesses, not choices. Because they can damage the heart and other organs, early treatment matters. With therapy, nutrition support, and sometimes medication, full recovery is possible.
symptoms: Intense fear of gaining weight or distorted body image
Severely limiting food, or episodes of binge eating
Vomiting, laxatives, or extreme exercise to "undo" eating
Eating in secret or withdrawing at mealtimes
Dizziness, fainting, or feeling cold all the time

drugs.name: Nutrition counseling & talk therapy
drugs.note: The foundation of treatment — restoring health and rebuilding a calm relationship with food.

drugs.name: Fluoxetine (Prozac)
drugs.note: FDA-approved for bulimia; reduces binge-purge cycles.

drugs.name: Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse)
drugs.note: FDA-approved for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder.

redFlags: Fainting, chest pain, or a very slow or irregular heartbeat needs emergency care — call 911 — and call or text 988 for thoughts of self-harm.

name: Sleep Apnea
overview: Sleep apnea is a condition where your breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep, often hundreds of times a night without you knowing. The most common type happens when throat muscles relax and block the airway, causing loud snoring and gasping. Left untreated, it raises the risk of high blood pressure, heart problems, and accidents from daytime sleepiness. The good news: treatment — most often a CPAP machine — works very well and can be life-changing.
symptoms: Pauses in breathing noticed by a bed partner
Daytime sleepiness even after a full night

drugs.name: CPAP machine
drugs.note: The first-choice treatment — gentle air pressure keeps the airway open all night.

drugs.name: Oral appliance
drugs.note: A dentist-made mouthpiece that holds the jaw forward; an option for milder cases.

drugs.name: Weight loss & side-sleeping
drugs.note: Even modest weight loss can noticeably reduce apnea episodes.

drugs.name: Tirzepatide (Zepbound)
drugs.note: A weight-loss medicine approved in 2024 for sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

redFlags: If you wake gasping with chest pain, or sleepiness is making you nod off behind the wheel, seek same-day medical care.

name: Pulmonary Embolism
prevalence: Up to ~900,000 U.S. blood-clot events (DVT/PE) each year
overview: A pulmonary embolism (PE) is a blood clot that blocks blood flow in the lungs, usually after forming in a leg vein and traveling upward. It can cause sudden shortness of breath and chest pain, and it is always a medical emergency. The encouraging news: with quick treatment, most people recover fully. Blood thinners stop the clot from growing while your body slowly dissolves it, and ongoing treatment helps prevent new clots from forming.
symptoms: Sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths
Swelling or pain in one leg (from the original clot)

drugs.name: Apixaban (Eliquis)
drugs.note: A common first-choice pill that stops the clot from growing.

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto)
drugs.note: Another widely used pill that works the same way.

drugs.name: Heparin / Enoxaparin (Lovenox)
drugs.note: Fast-acting; often started in the hospital.

drugs.name: Warfarin (Coumadin)
drugs.note: An older option that requires regular blood tests.

drugs.name: Clot-busting drugs (tPA)
drugs.note: Reserved for severe, life-threatening clots.

redFlags: Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood can signal a pulmonary embolism — call 911 right away.

name: RSV
prevalence: Nearly all U.S. kids catch it by age 2; tens of thousands hospitalized yearly
overview: RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) is a very common virus that infects the nose, throat, and lungs. For most people it feels like an ordinary cold, but it can be serious for babies, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems — sometimes causing breathing trouble that needs hospital care. There is no cure-all medicine; treatment is mostly rest, fluids, and fever relief. Newer vaccines and an antibody shot for infants now offer real protection.
symptoms: In babies: fussiness, poor feeding, or pauses in breathing

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases fever and aches while the virus runs its course.

drugs.name: Fluids & rest
drugs.note: The core of treatment — most cases clear up in a week or two.

drugs.name: Nirsevimab (Beyfortus)
drugs.note: A shot that protects babies during their first RSV season.

drugs.name: RSV vaccine (Arexvy, Abrysvo)
drugs.note: Recommended for older adults and during pregnancy to protect newborns.

redFlags: Call 911 or go to the ER if a child or adult is struggling to breathe, breathing very fast, has bluish lips, or a baby has long pauses in breathing.

name: Chronic Cough
overview: A chronic cough is one that lasts eight weeks or longer in adults. It is rarely a sign of something dangerous — the usual culprits are postnasal drip, asthma, acid reflux, or a common type of blood-pressure medicine (ACE inhibitors). Still, a lingering cough can disrupt sleep, work, and daily life. The key to fixing it is finding the cause; once that is treated, the vast majority of chronic coughs improve or disappear.
symptoms: A cough lasting 8 weeks or more
Frequent throat clearing or postnasal drip

drugs.name: Fluticasone (Flonase) nasal spray
drugs.note: Treats postnasal drip, the most common cause.

drugs.name: Omeprazole (Prilosec)
drugs.note: Helps when silent acid reflux is driving the cough.

drugs.name: Albuterol or inhaled steroid
drugs.note: Used when cough-variant asthma is to blame.

drugs.name: Dextromethorphan (Delsym)
drugs.note: Short-term relief while the underlying cause gets treated.

redFlags: Coughing up blood, chest pain, or worsening shortness of breath alongside a cough needs urgent care — go to the ER or seek same-day evaluation.

name: Lupus
overview: Lupus is an autoimmune disease, which means the body's defense system mistakenly attacks its own healthy tissue. It can affect the skin, joints, kidneys, heart, and more, and it tends to flare up and then quiet down. Most people with lupus are women, and it often starts between ages 15 and 44. There's no cure yet, but modern medicines control the disease so well that most people with lupus live full, active lives.
symptoms: Extreme tiredness that rest doesn't fix
A butterfly-shaped rash across the cheeks and nose

drugs.name: Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil)
drugs.note: The backbone of lupus care; gently calms the immune system.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: Quickly settles flares while other medicines take effect.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases joint pain and swelling.

drugs.name: Mycophenolate (CellCept)
drugs.note: Protects organs like the kidneys in more serious lupus.

drugs.name: Belimumab (Benlysta)
drugs.note: Targets the immune cells that drive lupus when standard treatment isn't enough.

redFlags: Chest pain, trouble breathing, new confusion, or a seizure during a lupus flare is an emergency — call 911.

name: Fibromyalgia
overview: Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain, deep fatigue, and trouble sleeping or concentrating (often called "fibro fog"). It isn't caused by joint damage — instead, the nervous system seems to turn up the volume on pain signals. It's real, it's common, and it affects women more often than men. While there's no cure, a mix of regular gentle exercise, good sleep habits, stress management, and certain medicines helps most people feel meaningfully better.
symptoms: Deep fatigue, even after a full night's sleep
Heightened sensitivity to touch, noise, or light

drugs.name: Regular low-impact exercise
drugs.note: Walking, swimming, or yoga is one of the most proven treatments.

drugs.name: Duloxetine (Cymbalta)
drugs.note: Eases pain while lifting mood and energy.

drugs.name: Pregabalin (Lyrica)
drugs.note: Calms overactive pain signals.

drugs.name: Amitriptyline
drugs.note: An older, low-cost option that can improve sleep and pain.

redFlags: Fibromyalgia doesn't cause hot swollen joints, high fever, or sudden weakness — those signs point to something else, so seek same-day care.

name: Psoriatic Arthritis
overview: Psoriatic arthritis is a form of arthritis that affects some people who have psoriasis, the skin condition that causes scaly, itchy patches. It can make joints stiff, swollen, and painful, and may cause sausage-like swelling of a finger or toe. Catching it early matters, because untreated inflammation can damage joints over time. The good news: today's medicines can calm the inflammation, protect the joints, and often clear the skin too.
symptoms: Sausage-like swelling of a finger or toe
Morning stiffness that lasts a while

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases mild joint pain and stiffness.

drugs.name: Methotrexate
drugs.note: A weekly medicine that slows joint inflammation.

drugs.name: Adalimumab (Humira)
drugs.note: Calms inflammation in both the joints and the skin.

drugs.name: Apremilast (Otezla)
drugs.note: A pill option often used for milder disease.

drugs.name: Secukinumab (Cosentyx)
drugs.note: Another biologic that treats joints and skin together.

redFlags: A single joint that is suddenly hot, very swollen, and paired with fever could be infected — seek same-day or emergency care.

name: Ankylosing Spondylitis
overview: Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis that mainly affects the spine, causing long-term inflammation in the back and hips. It usually starts in early adulthood with back pain and stiffness that's worse in the morning and better with movement — the opposite of a typical strained back. Over time it can cause bones in the spine to fuse, so early treatment and regular exercise matter. Today's medicines can ease pain and slow the disease itself.
symptoms: Low-back pain and stiffness, worst in the morning
Pain that improves with movement, not rest
Stiffness that wakes you late in the night
A gradually stooped posture over time

drugs.name: Naproxen / Ibuprofen
drugs.note: The first choice for easing pain and stiffness.

drugs.name: Physical therapy & daily stretching
drugs.note: Keeps the spine flexible and posture strong.

drugs.name: Adalimumab (Humira)
drugs.note: Used when NSAIDs aren't enough; slows the disease itself.

drugs.name: Secukinumab (Cosentyx)
drugs.note: An alternative biologic when TNF blockers aren't a fit.

redFlags: Severe back pain after even a minor fall, or new numbness with loss of bladder or bowel control, needs emergency care — go to the ER.

name: Erectile Dysfunction
overview: Erectile dysfunction (ED) means having trouble getting or keeping an erection firm enough for sex. It becomes more common with age, but it isn't an automatic part of getting older. ED is often linked to blood-flow problems, diabetes, stress, or certain medicines — so it can also be an early clue about heart health. The good news: it's very treatable, and pills like sildenafil work for most men. Talking with a doctor is the first step.
symptoms: Trouble keeping an erection during sex
Erections that are softer than they used to be
Stress or worry about sexual performance

drugs.name: Sildenafil (Viagra)
drugs.note: The best-known ED pill, taken before sex.

drugs.name: Tadalafil (Cialis)
drugs.note: Lasts longer and can also be taken daily.

drugs.name: Vardenafil (Levitra)
drugs.note: Works much like sildenafil.

drugs.name: Avanafil (Stendra)
drugs.note: A newer option that starts working quickly.

redFlags: An erection lasting more than four hours (priapism) can permanently damage the penis — go to the ER right away.

name: Overactive Bladder
overview: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a sudden, hard-to-control urge to urinate, often with frequent trips to the bathroom day and night. Some people also leak urine when the urge hits. OAB happens when the bladder muscle squeezes at the wrong times. It's common — especially with age — but it isn't something you just have to live with. Bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, and medicines help most people get back in control.
symptoms: Going more than 8 times a day
Waking up at night to urinate
Leaking urine when the urge hits

drugs.name: Bladder training & pelvic floor exercises
drugs.note: Usually the first step, and often enough on its own.

drugs.name: Oxybutynin (Ditropan)
drugs.note: Calms bladder muscle spasms.

drugs.name: Mirabegron (Myrbetriq)
drugs.note: Relaxes the bladder with less dry mouth than older drugs.

drugs.name: Tolterodine (Detrol)
drugs.note: An alternative that some people tolerate better.

redFlags: If you suddenly can't urinate at all, or have fever, back pain, or blood in your urine, seek same-day care.

name: Prostatitis
prevalence: Up to ~15% of U.S. men at some point
overview: Prostatitis is swelling or inflammation of the prostate, the small gland below a man's bladder. It can cause pelvic pain, burning with urination, and frequent urges to go. Some cases come from a bacterial infection and clear up with antibiotics; others, called chronic pelvic pain syndrome, last longer and need a mix of treatments. It's one of the most common urinary problems in men under 50, and most men improve with care.
symptoms: Pain in the pelvis, groin, or lower back
Frequent or urgent need to urinate

drugs.name: Ciprofloxacin
drugs.note: Treats bacterial prostatitis, often for several weeks.

drugs.name: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim)
drugs.note: A common alternative antibiotic.

drugs.name: Tamsulosin (Flomax)
drugs.note: Relaxes muscles near the prostate to ease urination.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen / Naproxen
drugs.note: Eases pain and inflammation.

redFlags: High fever, chills, and trouble urinating can signal acute bacterial prostatitis — go to the ER or seek same-day care.

name: Urinary Incontinence
overview: Urinary incontinence means leaking urine when you don't intend to — from a few drops with a cough or laugh to a sudden strong urge you can't hold. It's very common, especially in women after childbirth and in older adults, but it is not a normal part of aging you have to accept. Pelvic floor exercises, bladder training, and medicines help most people, and many improve a great deal.
symptoms: Leaking with coughs, sneezes, or exercise
Frequent bathroom trips day and night
Avoiding activities for fear of leaks

drugs.name: Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels)
drugs.note: The first-line treatment for stress-type leakage.

drugs.name: Bladder training
drugs.note: Gradually stretches the time between bathroom trips.

drugs.name: Oxybutynin (Ditropan)
drugs.note: Helps urge-type leakage by calming the bladder.

drugs.name: Mirabegron (Myrbetriq)
drugs.note: An alternative for urge leakage with less dry mouth.

drugs.name: Topical estrogen
drugs.note: Low-dose cream that can help some women after menopause.

redFlags: Sudden leakage along with numbness in the groin or legs, or loss of bowel control, can signal a spinal emergency — go to the ER.

name: Testicular Cancer
overview: Testicular cancer starts in a testicle, usually showing up as a painless lump or swelling. It mainly affects younger men, between about 15 and 44. While any cancer diagnosis is scary, this is one of the most curable cancers — more than 95% of men survive it, even when it has spread. Treatment usually starts with surgery to remove the affected testicle, sometimes followed by chemotherapy or radiation.
symptoms: A painless lump or swelling in a testicle
A testicle that feels heavier or firmer
Dull ache in the lower belly or groin
Sudden fluid buildup in the scrotum

drugs.name: Orchiectomy (surgery)
drugs.note: Removing the affected testicle is the main first treatment.

drugs.name: Cisplatin
drugs.note: The backbone of chemo when more than surgery is needed.

drugs.name: Etoposide
drugs.note: Usually given together with cisplatin.

drugs.name: Bleomycin
drugs.note: Part of the standard 'BEP' combination.

redFlags: Sudden, severe testicle pain may be testicular torsion — a different emergency that can cost the testicle — go to the ER immediately.
